title: Lesson F0.M1: Design with Simple Machines
heading: Overview
text:
Before choosing LEGO pieces or writing code, we can describe what the mission model needs to do. The aim here is to identify the input from the robot, the motion that input causes, and the output that earns the mission result. A motor's rotation or the robot's push may pass through several simple machines before the model moves.

For example, a motor may turn an axle that moves a short arm against a handle. Sketching that chain can show where the robot should touch the model and which part needs to move.

title: Lesson F0.M1: Design with Simple Machines
heading: Try the design lens
text:
Choose a practice model or make a small LEGO target. A drawing of its start and goal positions can help you decide whether it needs a push, pull, lift, rotation, or release. Mark a possible contact point and show the direction of the robot's force with an arrow. Then sketch a tool that could make that movement.

If the tool needs many moving parts, look again at the model's required motion. A simpler contact surface may be enough for the first test.

title: Lesson F0.M1: Design with Simple Machines
heading: Check and adjust
text: Your sketch should show the input, the motion through the tool, and the model's output. A teammate who has not seen your design may be able to point to the contact surface and predict what will move. If they cannot, the contact point or motion arrow may need another look.

title: Lesson F0.M2: What Simple Machines Do
heading: Overview
text:
The sketch from the previous lesson may include a lever, axle, or ramp. These are simple machines: they change how an applied force reaches a load. A longer input movement can produce a stronger push over a shorter distance, but the mechanism does not create energy. This lesson compares the six common types so we can recognize them in a mission tool.

| Simple machine | What it does | LEGO robot example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Lever** | Rotates around a pivot to move a load | A short arm lifts a handle. |
| **Wheel and axle** | Turns an axle and wheel together | Drive wheels move the robot; a gear fixed to an attachment axle passes rotation along. |
| **Pulley** | Guides a string or changes its pulling direction | A string routed over a pulley raises a light object. |
| **Inclined plane** | Spreads a lift over a longer path | A ramp guides an object upward. |
| **Wedge** | Pushes things apart or guides them sideways | A tapered guide centers an object as the robot approaches. |
| **Screw** | Turns rotation into travel along a thread | A threaded LEGO part can move a small piece gradually. |

Gears can change speed, turning direction, or torque between axles. A robot attachment may combine a motor, gears, an axle, and a lever. The table gives possible starting ideas; a test with the field model will show which motion is useful.

title: Lesson F0.M2: What Simple Machines Do
heading: Hands-on practice
text: A beam on a pivot makes a small lever. Moving the pivot closer to one end may change how far the other end travels for the same input. A wheel fixed to an axle should turn with it. Drawing an input and output arrow for each build can help you see the difference. A ruler on a pencil and a cardboard circle on a pencil can stand in for these two builds if LEGO parts are unavailable.

title: Lesson F0.M2: What Simple Machines Do
heading: Check and adjust
text: For each build, identify the simple machine and describe what changed in the motion or force. If it slips or binds, the pivot or axle supports may need attention before a motor would help.

title: Lesson F0.M3: Read Missions as Machines
heading: Overview
text:
Now that we can recognize simple machines, we can look for them in a mission model. The mission description gives the scoring goal, while the model shows the movement needed to reach it. Before choosing an attachment, study both the model itself and the robot's tool: identify the part that must move, its path, and a place where the tool could apply force.

| If the model must... | Look for... | First mechanism to try |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rotate a handle | Its pivot and required turning direction | A short lever on the robot that pushes the handle. |
| Raise a light piece | The lifting point and required height | A lever arm, or a string and pulley when the route allows it. |
| Slide an object into an area | The object's path and contact surface | A broad pusher, possibly with a wedge shaped guide. |
| Roll or carry an object | How it is held and released | Wheels and axles for approach, plus a small gate or lever for release. |

The mechanisms in the table are starting ideas. The current [FIRST Robot Game materials](https://www.firstinspires.org/resources/library/fll/season-materials) and the actual field model determine which actions are allowed and which ones score.

title: Lesson F0.M3: Read Missions as Machines
heading: Mission breakdown
text: For one model, describe the action in a sentence: “The robot applies [push, pull, or rotation] at [contact point], so [part] moves [distance or angle] toward [goal].” A sketch of the pivot, path, and nearby obstacles may reveal where a simple tool could make that action happen.

title: Lesson F0.M3: Read Missions as Machines
heading: Check and adjust
text: A gentle hand test should show whether the model moves in the direction your sketch predicts. If it moves another way or stops early, the sketch may need to change before you build a tool.

title: Lesson F0.M4: Build a Mission Mechanism
heading: Overview
text: The mission breakdown from F0.M3 gives us a contact point and a required motion. This lesson turns that sketch into one attachment we can test. The drive wheels may provide enough input for a fixed pusher or guide; a separate motor becomes useful when the tool must move without the robot driving.

title: Lesson F0.M4: Build a Mission Mechanism
heading: Build and test one action
text:
First decide whether the input will be a drive, a turn, or an attachment axle. A short lever could rotate a handle; a broad pusher or tapered guide could move a sliding object. The tool should reach the model before the hub or frame does and should leave room for the model's full motion.

One sturdy version is enough for a first test. Support the tool at more than one point on the frame, then move the robot slowly through the action by hand. Repeating three trials from the same launch position can show whether it contacts, moves, and releases the target in a repeatable way.

For a rotating handle, a short beam across its travel path may be enough. A forward drive would push the beam against the handle. If the beam slides off, changing its height or adding a small guide may help before adding another motor.

If you do not have a robot yet, a paper or cardboard mockup can still test the contact point and travel by hand.

title: Lesson F0.M4: Build a Mission Mechanism
heading: Check and adjust
text: The input, simple machine, contact point, and output should be visible in the build or sketch. If a trial fails, note the first missed contact or movement. Changing one dimension at a time can help you tell which adjustment made a difference.

title: Lesson F0.M5: Secure and Support the Robot
heading: Overview
text: A tool may reach the model once and miss it on the next run if its support moves. Before programming, we can check whether the robot frame and attachment keep the same shape under a gentle push. The aim is a contact point that stays in place across repeated starts.

title: Lesson F0.M5: Secure and Support the Robot
heading: Build checks
text:
Cross beams can help the left and right sides of the frame move together. The hub, motors, battery, and cables should stay clear of wheels and field models. Two spaced attachment points may keep a tool from twisting when it is pushed sideways, and fully seated pins make a swap easier to repeat.

A **cantilever** extends from one support with a load at its free end. A long unsupported wheel axle or tool may bend or twist. A second frame support, a shorter overhang, or a brace can help when the design needs reach. Turning each wheel and moving part by hand may reveal rubbing or binding before a powered test.

title: Lesson F0.M5: Secure and Support the Robot
heading: Quick reliability test
text: After lifting and setting down the robot by its frame, the tool should return to the same height and angle. A gentle push in the model's contact direction can show whether it twists. Three trials from one start mark may reveal movement that a single successful run hides. If the results vary, inspect loose connections and unsupported overhangs before changing the program.

title: Lesson F0.M5: Secure and Support the Robot
heading: Check and adjust
text: The load from the contact point needs a path back into the frame. If that path depends on one pin or a long unsupported beam, another support may improve repeatability. The mechanism is ready for the programming lessons when repeated runs keep it aligned.

title: Lesson F0.1: What FLL Challenge Is
heading: Overview
text: In FIRST LEGO League Challenge, the robot starts in a home area and runs without a driver during the Robot Game. We can use a short route to see how a program changes its position on the practice field. The aim here is to return to home after a drive and turn, then compare that simulated route with the current season's field rules.

title: Lesson F0.1: What FLL Challenge Is
heading: Worked example
text:
The [course port map](/fll/python-starter) is already loaded in the simulator editor. In this example, the robot drives away from home, turns around, and drives the same programmed distance back. On a physical build, the ports and dimensions would need to match your robot.

~~~python
print("Robot Game practice")
robot.straight(200)
robot.turn(180)
robot.straight(200)
~~~

title: Lesson F0.1: What FLL Challenge Is
heading: Simulator practice
text: The starter makes a short measured move. Watching its start and final pose can help you connect each code line with a field movement. After adding a return, the blue home area gives you a place to check whether the route ended where you expected.

title: Lesson F0.1: What FLL Challenge Is
heading: On the robot
text: The current [FIRST season materials](https://www.firstinspires.org/resources/library/fll/season-materials) should guide any physical Robot Game plan. Tracing this route from a chosen launch position without a tool can show whether the return would fit inside home on your field.

title: Lesson F0.1: What FLL Challenge Is
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The program determines the robot's moves, while the current rulebook determines what scores. If the final pose misses home, the first segment that differs from the plan may show where to adjust a distance or turn.

Reference: [FIRST season materials](https://www.firstinspires.org/resources/library/fll/season-materials).

title: Lesson F0.2: Set Up Pybricks and Telemark
heading: Overview
text:
The simulator can run the course's Python starter before a physical robot is ready. Pybricks Code runs a program on the SPIKE Prime Hub after Pybricks firmware is installed. This lesson lets us compare the two environments and identify the wiring and dimensions the starter assumes.

The course setup uses drive motors on ports A and B, a color sensor on C, an ultrasonic sensor on D, and an optional tool motor on E. Those ports and motor directions should match the real build. A program saved in Telemark stays in the browser; a Pybricks hub slot is a separate copy.

title: Lesson F0.2: Set Up Pybricks and Telemark
heading: Worked example
text:
The simulator editor already includes the course setup. The code below creates the hub, motors, sensors, and DriveBase before requesting a 100 mm drive. The 56 mm wheel diameter and 112 mm axle track are starter values that may need to change for a physical robot.

~~~python
from pybricks.hubs import PrimeHub
from pybricks.pupdevices import Motor, ColorSensor, UltrasonicSensor
from pybricks.parameters import Port, Direction
from pybricks.robotics import DriveBase

hub = PrimeHub()
left_motor = Motor(Port.A, Direction.COUNTERCLOCKWISE)
right_motor = Motor(Port.B)
robot = DriveBase(left_motor, right_motor, wheel_diameter=56, axle_track=112)
color_sensor = ColorSensor(Port.C)
distance_sensor = UltrasonicSensor(Port.D)
robot.straight(100)
~~~

title: Lesson F0.2: Set Up Pybricks and Telemark
heading: Simulator practice
text: The starter should move 100 mm in the simulator. A second run with `robot.straight(150)` can show how a 50 mm change affects the final position. Resetting between runs gives both versions the same start.

title: Lesson F0.2: Set Up Pybricks and Telemark
heading: On the robot
text: Installing Pybricks changes the hub firmware, so the [Pybricks installation guide](https://pybricks.com/learn/getting-started/install-pybricks/) should be followed with a mentor. The guide also explains how to restore LEGO firmware. For an initial motor test, the robot should have its wheels lifted and its ports checked against the program.

title: Lesson F0.2: Set Up Pybricks and Telemark
heading: Check and adjust
text:
You should be able to name the course port map and tell which copy of the program is in Telemark and which is on the hub. If the hub does not connect, firmware and Bluetooth permissions are useful first checks.

Reference: [Pybricks installation guide](https://pybricks.com/learn/getting-started/install-pybricks/).

title: Lesson F0.3: Drive a Measured Distance
heading: Overview
text: Now that the DriveBase is set up, we can ask it to travel a measured distance. `robot.straight(300)` requests 300 mm, or 30 cm, using the wheel encoders. The aim is to compare that command with how far the robot actually travels. Wheel slip or an incorrect wheel diameter may change the physical result.

title: Lesson F0.3: Drive a Measured Distance
heading: Worked example
text:
A positive distance drives forward. A negative distance drives backward, so the two calls below should finish near the starting point if both moves are accurate.

~~~python
robot.straight(300)
robot.straight(-300)
~~~

title: Lesson F0.3: Drive a Measured Distance
heading: Simulator practice
text: The example should move out and back in the simulator. Comparing one 300 mm move with two 150 mm moves can show whether the programmed distances end at the same pose. The physical robot may behave differently because stopping and starting can add error.

title: Lesson F0.3: Drive a Measured Distance
heading: On the robot
text: A 300 mm mark on a practice surface gives a reference for the command. Measuring from the same edge of the robot before and after three trials can show whether the actual travel is consistently short, long, or variable.

title: Lesson F0.3: Drive a Measured Distance
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The three trial records should include commanded distance, measured distance, and their difference. A consistent shortfall may point to wheel diameter or grip; variation between trials may call for a closer look at the surface and launch position.

Reference: [Pybricks DriveBase reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/robotics.html).

title: Lesson F0.4: Turn and Steer
heading: Overview
text: After driving a measured distance, we can change the robot's heading with `robot.turn()`. A positive angle requests a right turn and a negative angle requests a left turn. This lesson uses two turns to check where the robot faces after a short route. On a physical robot, axle track and wheel grip may affect the angle reached.

title: Lesson F0.4: Turn and Steer
heading: Worked example
text:
The first turn points the robot to its right for a 50 mm drive. The second turn points it back toward its original heading. If both turns are accurate, the route should end facing the same direction it started.

~~~python
robot.straight(200)
robot.turn(90)
robot.straight(50)
robot.turn(-90)
~~~

title: Lesson F0.4: Turn and Steer
heading: Simulator practice
text: The simulator shows the heading after each segment. With `robot.turn(-90)` at the end, the two turns cancel. Replacing that call with `robot.turn(90)` should leave the robot facing a different direction. A prediction before the second run can be checked against the field view.

title: Lesson F0.4: Turn and Steer
heading: On the robot
text: A tape mark can give the robot the same starting heading for three 90 degree right turns. Comparing the final headings may show a repeatable offset or variation caused by grip and alignment.

title: Lesson F0.4: Turn and Steer
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The final heading should follow from the two commanded turns. If the physical turn misses the mark in the same direction each time, the axle track value and wheel contact points are worth checking before changing the route.

Reference: [Pybricks DriveBase reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/robotics.html).

title: Lesson F0.5: Precision Route Challenge
heading: Overview
text: We have driven measured distances and made measured turns. This challenge combines them in a route that crosses the dark practice line and returns to the blue home area. The simulator checks for a line crossing, a turn, and a return without collision.

title: Lesson F0.5: Precision Route Challenge
heading: Worked example
text:
The 850 mm drive should cross the practice line in this simulator. A 180 degree turn points the robot back toward home, and the second drive requests the same distance in that direction. The numbers are a starting route to test, not measurements for a physical robot.

~~~python
robot.straight(850)
robot.turn(180)
robot.straight(850)
~~~

title: Lesson F0.5: Precision Route Challenge
heading: Simulator practice
text: The field view can show where the robot first crosses the line and where it ends after the return. If the example misses home, changing one distance or turn at a time can help identify the cause. Resetting between attempts keeps the starting pose the same.

title: Lesson F0.5: Precision Route Challenge
heading: On the robot
text: The same launch marks should be used for three physical trials. Measuring the final offset from the home target each time can show whether the route is close and repeatable enough to keep testing.

title: Lesson F0.5: Precision Route Challenge
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The simulator checks should confirm a line crossing, a measured turn, and a return home. On the mat, three recorded final positions may reveal a turn that needs separate testing from a marked heading.

Reference: [Pybricks DriveBase reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/robotics.html).

title: Lesson F1.1: Color and Reflected Light
heading: Overview
text:
Last unit, we drove measured distances. Now we can use reflected light as a signal to stop. The aim in this lesson is to stop with the color sensor over the dark practice line.

`color_sensor.reflection()` reports how much of the sensor's light a surface reflects, from 0% to 100%. The dark line should give a lower reading than the mat. If the readings are separated, a value between them may work as a stopping threshold. The example below uses 35, but the value for your robot may differ with sensor height and surface finish.

title: Lesson F1.1: Color and Reflected Light
heading: Worked example
text:
`robot.drive(100, 0)` starts a straight drive at 100 mm/s. The 10 ms wait spaces out the sensor readings as long as the sensor reading stays above 35. If a reading reaches 35 or less, Python leaves the loop and runs `robot.stop()`.

~~~python
print("Light:", color_sensor.reflection())
robot.drive(100, 0)
while color_sensor.reflection() > 35:
    wait(10)
robot.stop()
~~~

If the sensor never reads 35 or less, this loop will keep driving. The next lesson adds a time limit for that case.

title: Lesson F1.1: Color and Reflected Light
heading: Simulator practice
text: The starter prints one reflection reading before the drive and another near the line after a 750 mm move. A threshold between those readings is a starting point for replacing the fixed drive with the loop above. After running it, check whether the sensor stops over the line.

title: Lesson F1.1: Color and Reflected Light
heading: On the robot
text: The real sensor should stay at its normal mounting height while you collect readings from the mat and the line. Five readings on each surface will show whether there is a useful gap between them. Once you have a threshold in that gap, testing three line stops can show how consistently it works.

title: Lesson F1.1: Color and Reflected Light
heading: Check and adjust
text:
A useful threshold should put the mat and line readings on opposite sides of it. The stopping point may still change between runs, so compare the three trials before relying on it. If the readings overlap, check the sensor height and measure again.

Reference: [Pybricks ColorSensor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/colorsensor.html).

title: Lesson F1.2: Distance and Wait Until
heading: Overview
text:
The line stop in the previous lesson depends on seeing the line. We can also use a distance reading to stop before an obstacle. The aim here is to stop when the ultrasonic sensor reads 150 mm or less, with a three-second time limit if that reading never arrives.

`distance_sensor.distance()` reports millimeters. It returns 2000 when there is no valid reading, so the distance condition may remain true even if no object is detected. `StopWatch.time()` reports elapsed milliseconds. In the example, both conditions must remain true for the drive to continue.

title: Lesson F1.2: Distance and Wait Until
heading: Worked example
text:
The stopwatch starts before `robot.drive(100, 0)`, and the 10 ms wait spaces out the readings. If the sensor reports 150 mm or less, or 3000 ms pass, Python leaves the loop and calls `robot.stop()`. The final line prints the distance reported at that point.

~~~python
watch = StopWatch()
robot.drive(100, 0)
while distance_sensor.distance() > 150 and watch.time() < 3000:
    wait(10)
robot.stop()
print("Range:", distance_sensor.distance())
~~~

title: Lesson F1.2: Distance and Wait Until
heading: Simulator practice
text: The simulator has an obstacle directly ahead. With the starter code, the distance reading should end the drive first. With `100` in place of `3000`, the timer should end a second run first. The printed distance and final position can help you compare the two stopping conditions.

title: Lesson F1.2: Distance and Wait Until
heading: On the robot
text: The sensor should stay at the height and angle it will use in the route. A ruler measurement after the stop can show whether a 150 mm sensor reading leaves enough room in front of the chassis. A broad target and an angled target may give different readings, so testing both can help you choose a threshold for your field.

title: Lesson F1.2: Distance and Wait Until
heading: Check and adjust
text:
Both the range reading and the timer should be able to end the loop. If the robot continues driving after the expected stop, check the printed distance, the elapsed time, and whether `robot.stop()` is outside the loop.

Reference: [Pybricks UltrasonicSensor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/ultrasonicsensor.html).

title: Lesson F1.3: Hub Heading and Reset
heading: Overview
text:
After stopping at a line or an obstacle, a heading reading can help us check the robot's direction. The aim in this lesson is to reset heading to zero, command a 90 degree right turn, and compare the reading with that command.

The Prime Hub IMU reports heading in degrees relative to its starting or reset direction. Positive values mean clockwise turns. The hub should stay fixed in a known orientation so the reading describes the robot's turn. Heading should be reset while the robot is stopped. If the DriveBase is using gyro control, use `robot.reset(angle=0)` instead of `hub.imu.reset_heading(0)`.

title: Lesson F1.3: Hub Heading and Reset
heading: Worked example
text:
The starter setup does not enable gyro control, so this example resets the IMU directly. `robot.stop()` runs first, and `hub.imu.reset_heading(0)` makes the current direction zero. After `robot.turn(90)`, the final line prints the IMU's estimate of the turn.

~~~python
robot.stop()
hub.imu.reset_heading(0)
robot.turn(90)
print("Heading:", hub.imu.heading())
~~~

title: Lesson F1.3: Hub Heading and Reset
heading: Simulator practice
text: The starter runs the right turn and prints its heading. The field view also shows the robot's direction. A second run with `robot.turn(-90)` should give a negative reading after the reset. Comparing both readings with the field view can help you check the sign of each turn.

title: Lesson F1.3: Hub Heading and Reset
heading: On the robot
text: The hub should remain fixed to the robot during these tests. A mark on the practice mat can give you the same starting direction for three right turns. Comparing each printed heading with 90 degrees may reveal a repeatable error or variation between runs. If the sign is unexpected, check how the hub is mounted.

title: Lesson F1.3: Hub Heading and Reset
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The heading should be positive after a right turn and negative after a left turn. The difference between a reading and the commanded angle gives the error for that run. One close result may not tell you how the next turn will end, so compare all three trials.

Reference: [Pybricks PrimeHub reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/hubs/primehub.html).

title: Lesson F1.4: Attachment Motors and Objects
heading: Overview
text:
We can now use sensors to stop the robot and check its heading after a turn. The next piece is the attachment that will handle a mission object. The aim in this lesson is to rotate its motor through a known angle and bring it back to its starting position.

`Motor.run_angle(speed, rotation_angle)` takes speed in degrees per second and a relative rotation in motor degrees. A positive angle turns the motor one way; a negative angle reverses it. Which way the tool moves depends on how the motor and gears are mounted.

title: Lesson F1.4: Attachment Motors and Objects
heading: Worked example
text:
The first call asks the motor to turn 90 degrees at 200 degrees per second. The second asks it to turn back by the same amount. If the mechanism moves freely, the tool should return close to where it started. A gear train may make the tool's angle different from the motor's angle.

~~~python
attachment = Motor(Port.E)
attachment.run_angle(200, 90)
attachment.run_angle(200, -90)
~~~

title: Lesson F1.4: Attachment Motors and Objects
heading: Simulator practice
text: The starter contains the two motor moves from the example. In the simulator, the attachment should rise and return. Watching its motion can help you check the direction and size of the command before using the tool near the red cargo in the next challenge.

title: Lesson F1.4: Attachment Motors and Objects
heading: On the robot
text: The real tool should be tested with the robot lifted so it can move freely. Short moves of 30, 60, and 90 motor degrees can help you find an angle that reaches the object without pressing against the frame or a hard stop. The angle you use in the mission route should come from those tests.

title: Lesson F1.4: Attachment Motors and Objects
heading: Check and adjust
text:
A useful angle should let the tool return without striking the frame or holding against a hard stop. If it binds, reduce the travel and inspect the clearance before trying a faster move. The motor angle alone may not tell you where the tool ends up.

Reference: [Pybricks Motor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/motor.html).

title: Lesson F1.5: Retrieve and Deliver Challenge
heading: Overview
text:
We have used a sensor reading to stop the robot and a motor angle to move its attachment. The aim of this challenge is to collect the red cargo and release it inside the green delivery area. The simulator checks for a sensor reading, an attachment move, and a delivery without collision.

In the simulator, the robot needs to be near the cargo when the attachment rises. If it picks up the cargo, the object moves with the robot until the attachment lowers near its starting angle. A release inside the green area should count as a delivery.

title: Lesson F1.5: Retrieve and Deliver Challenge
heading: Worked example
text:
This fragment shows a line stop followed by an attachment move and release. The 500 mm drive is an example segment. To use it for the challenge, you will need measured moves that bring the robot near the cargo before pickup and into the delivery area before release.

~~~python
robot.drive(100, 0)
while color_sensor.reflection() > 35:
    wait(10)
robot.stop()
attachment.run_angle(200, 90)
robot.straight(500)
attachment.run_angle(200, -90)
~~~

title: Lesson F1.5: Retrieve and Deliver Challenge
heading: Simulator practice
text:
The simulator starts the robot in the home area. A route should bring it near the red cargo before raising the attachment and into the green delivery area before lowering it. It should also read either the color or ultrasonic sensor.

If the cargo stays behind, the robot may be too far away or the attachment may not have risen enough. If the cargo moves with the robot but delivery does not count, check where it was released and whether the attachment lowered far enough.

title: Lesson F1.5: Retrieve and Deliver Challenge
heading: On the robot
text: The first physical trials should use reduced speed. Recording the pickup and release positions across three runs can show whether they repeat. The simulator's distances may give you a starting point, but the final angles and drive lengths should come from tests with your tool and field.

title: Lesson F1.5: Retrieve and Deliver Challenge
heading: Check and adjust
text:
All three simulator checks should pass before you try the route on the practice mat. On the mat, check whether the object stays inside the delivery area across the trials. If a run misses, finding out whether the error happened at pickup or release can help you choose which distance or angle to change.

If the line stop needs work, return to [Color and Reflected Light](/fll/unit-01/color-and-reflected-light). For the tool angle, see [Attachment Motors and Objects](/fll/unit-01/attachment-motors).

Reference: [Pybricks ColorSensor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/colorsensor.html).

title: Lesson F2.1: Python Functions and Parameters
heading: Overview
text: We have used individual drive commands for each route. A function lets us name a move and call it with different distances. Here we will make one distance function and use it twice, so the distance at each call is easy to find. A parameter such as `distance_mm` also makes its unit clear to a teammate.

title: Lesson F2.1: Python Functions and Parameters
heading: Worked example
text:
`drive_mm` takes a distance in millimeters and passes it to `robot.straight()`. The first call requests 200 mm. After the turn, the second call requests 50 mm without changing the function itself.

~~~python
def drive_mm(distance_mm):
    robot.straight(distance_mm)

drive_mm(200)
robot.turn(90)
drive_mm(50)
~~~

title: Lesson F2.1: Python Functions and Parameters
heading: Simulator practice
text: The starter has one drive and one turn command. Adding `drive_mm` from the example and calling it before and after the turn creates two segments to compare. Changing only one argument can show which segment that call controls.

title: Lesson F2.1: Python Functions and Parameters
heading: On the robot
text: A repeated drive or tool action may be easier to adjust in Pybricks Code when it has one named function. Two calls with different arguments can show whether the function gives the expected motion for both values.

title: Lesson F2.1: Python Functions and Parameters
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The function definition should describe one action, while each call supplies the value for that action. If only one segment has the wrong distance, its argument is a useful first place to check.

Reference: [Pybricks first robot program](https://pybricks.com/learn/making-programs/your-first-program/).

title: Lesson F2.2: Launch Marks and Home
heading: Overview
text: The route from the last lesson depends on where the robot starts. This lesson uses two physical marks to give each launch the same position and heading, then checks whether a short route can return home. A repeated starting pose may make differences in the route easier to interpret.

title: Lesson F2.2: Launch Marks and Home
heading: Worked example
text:
`run_short_mission()` drives 250 mm, turns, makes a short side move, and reverses that side move. The final turn and reverse drive request a return to the original pose. This only works as a field route if the return path stays clear.

~~~python
def run_short_mission():
    robot.straight(250)
    robot.turn(90)
    robot.straight(50)
    robot.straight(-50)
    robot.turn(-90)
    robot.straight(-250)

run_short_mission()
~~~

title: Lesson F2.2: Launch Marks and Home
heading: Simulator practice
text: A drawing of the outgoing and return segments can help you predict the final pose before running the code. In the simulator, compare that prediction with the blue home boundary. If the route misses, note which segment first differs from the drawing.

title: Lesson F2.2: Launch Marks and Home
heading: On the robot
text: Two marks for the same chassis edges can make the physical launch position easier to repeat. Marking the final position after five starts may show whether the route ends in one area or spreads across the mat.

title: Lesson F2.2: Launch Marks and Home
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The launch notes should let another teammate place the robot the same way. If the five final positions vary, check the launch marks and alignment before changing the route.

Reference: [FIRST season materials](https://www.firstinspires.org/resources/library/fll/season-materials).

title: Lesson F2.3: Calibration and Repeatability
heading: Overview
text: One run near a target does not tell us whether the route repeats. This lesson compares several 500 mm drives so we can tell a consistent shortfall from variation between runs. A consistent offset may point to a wheel dimension; scattered endpoints may point to grip, launch alignment, or loose parts.

title: Lesson F2.3: Calibration and Repeatability
heading: Worked example
text:
The constants give the DriveBase a wheel diameter and axle track in millimeters. `robot.straight(500)` then uses those values to estimate travel. The simulator can vary wheel calibration between profiles, while a physical test can help us decide whether the values fit the actual build.

~~~python
WHEEL_DIAMETER_MM = 56
AXLE_TRACK_MM = 112
robot = DriveBase(left_motor, right_motor,
                  wheel_diameter=WHEEL_DIAMETER_MM,
                  axle_track=AXLE_TRACK_MM)
robot.straight(500)
~~~

title: Lesson F2.3: Calibration and Repeatability
heading: Simulator practice
text: The simulator's calibration table shows how the same code ends under three wheel profiles. Comparing those endpoints after a 500 mm drive can reveal whether a route is sensitive to a small wheel difference. Repeating an unchanged run should give the same simulated result for each profile.

title: Lesson F2.3: Calibration and Repeatability
heading: On the robot
text: Wheel diameter and the spacing between wheel contact points are starting measurements for the real DriveBase. Five 500 mm trials with unchanged code can show whether the robot has a repeatable bias or run-to-run scatter.

title: Lesson F2.3: Calibration and Repeatability
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The trial notes should separate a similar miss on every run from a miss that changes size or direction. A stable bias may justify a measured geometry adjustment; scatter calls for checking grip and loose parts first.

Reference: [Pybricks DriveBase reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/robotics.html).

title: Lesson F2.4: Mission Order, Recovery, and Time
heading: Overview
text: The Robot Game lasts 150 seconds, including launches and attachment changes. We can time a short mission and use that result to decide what may fit after it. The aim here is a mission order with room to return or recover if the first attempt takes longer than expected.

title: Lesson F2.4: Mission Order, Recovery, and Time
heading: Worked example
text:
`StopWatch()` begins timing before the drive and attachment move. The final print reports the program's elapsed milliseconds after the return command. This does not include the team's time between launches, so a match plan needs a separate allowance for that work.

~~~python
watch = StopWatch()
robot.straight(300)
attachment.run_angle(200, 90)
robot.straight(-300)
print("Mission ms:", watch.time())
~~~

title: Lesson F2.4: Mission Order, Recovery, and Time
heading: Simulator practice
text: The simulator can time two candidate routes. Adding a five-second setup allowance per launch gives a fuller estimate of each plan. A route with fewer chances to miss may be a better first choice even if its simulated score is lower.

title: Lesson F2.4: Mission Order, Recovery, and Time
heading: On the robot
text: Five physical runs with the same attachment can show how much the route time varies. The median and longest time give different planning numbers; the longest run may be more useful when deciding how much recovery time to reserve.

title: Lesson F2.4: Mission Order, Recovery, and Time
heading: Check and adjust
text:
A usable plan should fit within 150 seconds after its setup and recovery allowances. If the estimate exceeds that limit, dropping an objective may leave enough time for a return. The plan should state which objective the team would skip if time runs short.

Reference: [Pybricks timing tools reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/tools/).

title: Lesson F2.5: First Mission Run Capstone
heading: Overview
text: The first mission run brings the earlier pieces together. The simulator checks whether the robot activates the target, delivers the object, and returns home within 150 seconds without a collision. Functions can keep the target action and return route separate while you test each part.

title: Lesson F2.5: First Mission Run Capstone
heading: Worked example
text:
The [course port map](/fll/python-starter) supplies the device names below. `target_action()` and `return_home()` show how two route parts can be named. This fragment does not reach every field objective by itself; a complete route needs a pickup and delivery action at the corresponding field positions.

~~~python
def target_action():
    robot.straight(250)
    attachment.run_angle(180, 90)
    attachment.run_angle(180, -90)

def return_home():
    robot.turn(180)
    robot.straight(250)

target_action()
return_home()
~~~

title: Lesson F2.5: First Mission Run Capstone
heading: Simulator practice
text: The field view can help you place the target action, pickup, and release along one route. The three simulator checks should show target activation, delivery, and a return home within 150 seconds. Keeping the launch pose fixed between attempts makes route changes easier to compare.

title: Lesson F2.5: First Mission Run Capstone
heading: On the robot
text: On a practice field, three runs from the same launch marks may show whether the target and delivery actions repeat. Record the first missed position in each run before deciding what to change.

title: Lesson F2.5: First Mission Run Capstone
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The simulator checks should pass before a physical run is treated as a match plan. The notes from three mat trials can show whether a miss begins at the target, the cargo pickup, the release, or the return. A function for the first missed action can be tested on its own.

Reference: [FIRST season materials](https://www.firstinspires.org/resources/library/fll/season-materials).

title: Lesson F3.1: Numbers, Booleans, and Text
heading: Overview
text: The route now has numbers we may need to change. Python can store those numbers alongside Boolean values such as `True` and text such as `"launch"`. This lesson compares those value types so we can choose a distance for a drive and print a useful label with it. A number inside quotes is text and cannot be used directly in arithmetic.

title: Lesson F3.1: Numbers, Booleans, and Text
heading: Worked example
text:
`distance_mm` and `turn_deg` hold numbers, `at_home` holds a Boolean, and `label` holds text. The print line shows all four values, while `robot.straight()` uses the numeric distance. Changing the label should affect the output without changing the drive.

~~~python
distance_mm = 300
turn_deg = 90
at_home = True
label = "launch"
print(label, distance_mm, "mm", at_home)
robot.straight(distance_mm)
~~~

title: Lesson F3.1: Numbers, Booleans, and Text
heading: Simulator practice
text: The starter drives using `distance_mm`. A second run with 450 instead of 300 should end farther from the start. Adding the print line from the example can help you check that the value sent to the drive matches the one you intended.

title: Lesson F3.1: Numbers, Booleans, and Text
heading: On the robot
text: Before a physical drive, printing the planned distance with `mm` beside it can help catch a value in the wrong unit. A Boolean such as `at_home` may also be useful when you later add a condition to a route.

title: Lesson F3.1: Numbers, Booleans, and Text
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The printed values should make it possible to identify which entries are numbers, text, and Booleans. If a distance calculation fails, a quoted number such as `"300"` may be the cause.

Reference: [Pybricks first robot program](https://pybricks.com/learn/making-programs/your-first-program/).

title: Lesson F3.2: Variables and Units
heading: Overview
text: Once a value has a name, its unit should be clear too. DriveBase distances use millimeters, while a field measurement may be written in centimeters. In this lesson we will convert a 30 cm target to 300 mm once, then use the converted value for the drive. A name such as `target_mm` can help keep the two units apart.

title: Lesson F3.2: Variables and Units
heading: Worked example
text:
`TARGET_CM * 10` converts centimeters to millimeters. The print line exposes the converted value before `robot.straight(target_mm)` uses it. The speed and turn settings use their own units, shown in the code comment.

~~~python
TARGET_CM = 30
target_mm = TARGET_CM * 10
speed_mm_s = 150
print("Target:", target_mm, "mm")
robot.settings(speed_mm_s, 300, 90, 180)  # mm/s, mm/s², deg/s, deg/s²
robot.straight(target_mm)
~~~

title: Lesson F3.2: Variables and Units
heading: Simulator practice
text: A second run with `TARGET_CM = 40` should send 400 mm to `robot.straight()`. The printed target and final pose can help you check that the conversion happened once.

title: Lesson F3.2: Variables and Units
heading: On the robot
text: A centimeter measurement from the practice mat should be converted before it is used by the DriveBase. Writing both values in a notebook can make a tenfold unit error easier to notice when you compare the route with tape marks.

title: Lesson F3.2: Variables and Units
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The code's `target_mm` and the notebook's converted value should agree. If a 30 cm plan commands only 30 mm, the missing factor of ten is a useful first check.

Reference: [Pybricks DriveBase reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/robotics.html).

title: Lesson F3.3: Arithmetic for Motion
heading: Overview
text: A robot tool may need to stop before it reaches a model. We can calculate that approach distance from a measured gap and a tool clearance. This lesson uses one subtraction in millimeters so the drive command can follow a measurement rather than a guessed constant.

title: Lesson F3.3: Arithmetic for Motion
heading: Worked example
text:
The field gap is 420 mm and the chosen tool clearance is 55 mm. Subtracting gives an approach command of 365 mm. Printing `approach_mm` makes the number visible when you compare the result with the field.

~~~python
field_gap_mm = 420
tool_clearance_mm = 55
approach_mm = field_gap_mm - tool_clearance_mm
robot.straight(approach_mm)
print("Approach:", approach_mm, "mm")
~~~

title: Lesson F3.3: Arithmetic for Motion
heading: Simulator practice
text: Increasing the clearance to 70 mm should shorten the approach to 350 mm. Predicting that value before a second simulator run can help you check whether the calculation and final pose agree.

title: Lesson F3.3: Arithmetic for Motion
heading: On the robot
text: The real field gap and tool reach should be measured from fixed reference points. A clearance chosen from those measurements may leave room for the attachment to act without the chassis touching the model.

title: Lesson F3.3: Arithmetic for Motion
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The printed approach distance should equal the measured gap minus the chosen clearance. If the robot stops too close to the model, check where both measurements were taken before changing the subtraction.

Reference: [Pybricks DriveBase reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/robotics.html).

title: Lesson F3.4: Print Useful Diagnostics
heading: Overview
text: We have printed values to inspect a route. A reading is more useful when its label says where it was taken and what unit it uses. Here we will print the launch range, a heading after a drive, and reflected light so a later run can be compared line by line.

title: Lesson F3.4: Print Useful Diagnostics
heading: Worked example
text:
Each `print()` call puts a route point or measurement name beside the value. `distance_sensor.distance()` reports millimeters and `hub.imu.heading()` reports degrees. The text labels do not change the robot's motion; they help explain the output after the drive.

~~~python
print("launch range mm:", distance_sensor.distance())
robot.straight(200)
print("after 200 mm, heading deg:", hub.imu.heading())
print("reflection percent:", color_sensor.reflection())
~~~

title: Lesson F3.4: Print Useful Diagnostics
heading: Simulator practice
text: The example should produce three labeled lines. After a different straight distance, comparing those lines from the same start may show which readings changed with the robot's position.

title: Lesson F3.4: Print Useful Diagnostics
heading: On the robot
text: On the physical robot, the same labels can make a test log easier to match with the route. Moving the robot by hand before a drive may show which sensor values respond to position or heading changes.

title: Lesson F3.4: Print Useful Diagnostics
heading: Check and adjust
text:
A useful log entry should include enough context to identify the reading later. If two values look alike but were taken at different places, the route-point labels may explain the difference.

Reference: [Pybricks timing tools reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/tools/).

title: Lesson F3.5: Data Check Challenge
heading: Overview
text: This challenge brings together a named distance, a unit conversion, and a drive. The simulator checks that a Python variable reaches `robot.straight()`, the robot finishes near the 300 mm target, and the route avoids a collision. Printing the planned and estimated distances can help explain a miss.

title: Lesson F3.5: Data Check Challenge
heading: Worked example
text:
`target_cm * 10` converts 30 cm to 300 mm. After the drive, `robot.distance()` reports the DriveBase estimate. Subtracting the target gives an encoder-based error, which may differ from the physical distance measured on a mat.

~~~python
target_cm = 30
target_mm = target_cm * 10
robot.reset()
robot.straight(target_mm)
error_mm = robot.distance() - target_mm
print("target mm:", target_mm)
print("encoder error mm:", error_mm)
~~~

title: Lesson F3.5: Data Check Challenge
heading: Simulator practice
text: Changing `target_cm` should change the converted value without editing `robot.straight(target_mm)`. The check for a final position near 300 mm will pass only when the chosen value brings the robot back near that target.

title: Lesson F3.5: Data Check Challenge
heading: On the robot
text: Three physical drives from the same mark can give you both encoder estimates and ruler measurements. Comparing them may reveal wheel slip even when the printed encoder error is small.

title: Lesson F3.5: Data Check Challenge
heading: Check and adjust
text:
For a 30 cm plan, the printed target should be 300 mm. The log should keep encoder error separate from the difference measured with a ruler. A small encoder error alongside a physical miss may point to slip or an incorrect wheel diameter.

Reference: [Pybricks DriveBase reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/robotics.html).

title: Lesson F4.1: Compare Sensor Readings
heading: Overview
text: After reading a sensor, we can compare its value with a threshold. The comparison gives `True` or `False`, which a program can use to choose an action. This lesson tests a range threshold in millimeters, including the exact boundary where the result changes.

title: Lesson F4.1: Compare Sensor Readings
heading: Worked example
text:
`too_close` is true only when `range_mm` is less than 150. A reading of exactly 150 gives `False` because the operator is `<`. Printing the reading and Boolean before the `if` makes that boundary visible.

~~~python
range_mm = distance_sensor.distance()
too_close = range_mm < 150
print("Range mm:", range_mm)
print("Too close:", too_close)
if too_close:
    robot.stop()
~~~

title: Lesson F4.1: Compare Sensor Readings
heading: Simulator practice
text: Values of 149, 150, and 151 mm should give `True`, `False`, and `False` for this comparison. Trying those values in a short Python list can show the boundary before you compare the simulator's fixed obstacle reading.

title: Lesson F4.1: Compare Sensor Readings
heading: On the robot
text: On the physical robot, the measured gap at the moment the condition changes may differ from the sensor reading. The sensor's position on the chassis should be included when you compare that gap with 150 mm.

title: Lesson F4.1: Compare Sensor Readings
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The printed Boolean should change at the boundary you chose. If it changes at an unexpected physical gap, check the units and sensor mounting position before changing the number.

Reference: [Pybricks UltrasonicSensor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/ultrasonicsensor.html).

title: Lesson F4.2: Choose One Branch
heading: Overview
text: One sensor comparison can choose between two outcomes. With `if`, `elif`, and `else`, the robot can choose one of several actions in priority order. Here a close obstacle should stop the route before a dark-line reading can trigger a turn; a clear field allows a short drive.

title: Lesson F4.2: Choose One Branch
heading: Worked example
text:
Python checks `range_mm < 150` first. It checks the line reading only if that first condition is false, and it runs the `else` block only if neither condition is true. The printed word can show which branch ran in a test.

~~~python
range_mm = distance_sensor.distance()
light = color_sensor.reflection()
if range_mm < 150:
    robot.stop()
    print("stop")
elif light < 35:
    robot.turn(90)
    print("line")
else:
    robot.straight(100)
    print("clear")
~~~

title: Lesson F4.2: Choose One Branch
heading: Simulator practice
text: The simulator field can stay fixed while you change a threshold to make each branch run in turn. The output should show `stop`, `line`, or `clear`, with only one of those words per run. Restoring the chosen thresholds afterward lets you test the intended priority.

title: Lesson F4.2: Choose One Branch
heading: On the robot
text: The first physical tests should keep the wheels lifted while you compare printed readings and branches. Low-speed mat trials can then show whether the chosen thresholds match the real obstacle and line.

title: Lesson F4.2: Choose One Branch
heading: Check and adjust
text:
A useful test log should include one case for each printed result. If more than one action appears in a run, check the indentation and whether the actions belong to a single `if`/`elif`/`else` chain.

Reference: [Pybricks UltrasonicSensor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/ultrasonicsensor.html).

title: Lesson F4.3: Combine Conditions
heading: Overview
text: We can now combine sensor comparisons into one decision. `and` requires both conditions, `or` accepts either, and `not` reverses a Boolean. This lesson uses a nearby object and a light surface as the two requirements for moving an attachment. Naming each result can make the combined condition easier to read.

title: Lesson F4.3: Combine Conditions
heading: Worked example
text:
`near_object` and `on_dark_line` are calculated separately. `safe_to_pick` is true only when the object is near and the sensor is away from the dark line. If either part fails, the example prints a message instead of moving the tool.

~~~python
near_object = distance_sensor.distance() < 160
on_dark_line = color_sensor.reflection() < 35
safe_to_pick = near_object and not on_dark_line
if safe_to_pick:
    attachment.run_angle(180, 60)
else:
    print("Pickup condition failed")
~~~

title: Lesson F4.3: Combine Conditions
heading: Simulator practice
text: There are four possible pairs of values for two Booleans. Testing each pair before reading the field sensors can show that only `True` for `near_object` and `False` for `on_dark_line` moves the tool.

title: Lesson F4.3: Combine Conditions
heading: On the robot
text: Before powering the physical tool, its path should be clear even when `safe_to_pick` is true. The Boolean checks sensor values; they cannot detect every object that might block the attachment.

title: Lesson F4.3: Combine Conditions
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The tool should move only for the intended combination. If it moves at another time, the printed intermediate Booleans may show which comparison gave an unexpected result.

Reference: [Pybricks ColorSensor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/colorsensor.html).

title: Lesson F4.4: Avoid Threshold Chatter
heading: Overview
text: A reflected-light reading may hover around one threshold while the robot is near the edge of a line. Two thresholds can keep the state from switching on every small change. In this lesson, a reading below 30% enters the dark state, and a reading above 40% leaves it. The previous state must be kept between readings for that gap to work.

title: Lesson F4.4: Avoid Threshold Chatter
heading: Worked example
text:
This fragment shows one update to `on_line`. A light reading between 30% and 40% leaves the state as it was. To test several readings, the same `on_line` variable needs to be reused rather than reset to `False` before each reading.

~~~python
light = color_sensor.reflection()
on_line = False
if not on_line and light < 30:
    on_line = True
elif on_line and light > 40:
    on_line = False
print("On line:", on_line)
~~~

title: Lesson F4.4: Avoid Threshold Chatter
heading: Simulator practice
text: The sequence 50, 29, 35, and 41 percent should produce states of light, dark, dark, and light when the state persists. A loop over those values can test the rule before you compare it with readings from the simulator line.

title: Lesson F4.4: Avoid Threshold Chatter
heading: On the robot
text: Five readings on each physical surface may show how much they vary. A gap between the two thresholds should be wider than ordinary variation near the line edge, while still separating the surfaces you need to detect.

title: Lesson F4.4: Avoid Threshold Chatter
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The state should hold steady for readings between 30% and 40%. If it changes repeatedly at an edge on the physical mat, the measured variation may call for a wider gap or a steadier sensor height.

Reference: [Pybricks ColorSensor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/colorsensor.html).

title: Lesson F4.5: Decision Challenge
heading: Overview
text: This challenge combines a distance reading, a line reading, and a time limit in one approach. The aim is a route that stops before a collision and prints which condition ended it. The simulator checks for an ultrasonic reading, an `if` decision, and a stop without collision.

title: Lesson F4.5: Decision Challenge
heading: Worked example
text:
`reason` starts as `"timeout"`. Each sensor can replace that word and break out of the loop; otherwise the four-second limit ends the loop. `robot.stop()` sits after the loop, so every exit reaches the stop call.

~~~python
watch = StopWatch()
reason = "timeout"
robot.drive(100, 0)
while watch.time() < 4000:
    if distance_sensor.distance() < 150:
        reason = "obstacle"
        break
    if color_sensor.reflection() < 35:
        reason = "line"
        break
    wait(10)
robot.stop()
print(reason)
~~~

title: Lesson F4.5: Decision Challenge
heading: Simulator practice
text: With the field fixed, changing thresholds and the timeout can make `obstacle`, `line`, and `timeout` appear in separate runs. Each run should stop. The threshold values used for the final route should come from the readings observed on the practice field.

title: Lesson F4.5: Decision Challenge
heading: On the robot
text: Low-speed mat trials can show whether each printed reason matches the physical stop point. A clear lane is useful for testing the timeout without putting an obstacle in the robot's path.

title: Lesson F4.5: Decision Challenge
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The program should stop for all three reasons. If the no-cue run lasts longer than planned, check that the timer is advancing and that the stop call follows the loop.

Reference: [Pybricks timing tools reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/tools/).

title: Lesson F5.1: Repeat a Known Count
heading: Overview
text: Some tests need the same movement more than once. A `for` loop repeats a known number of times, and `range(3)` gives the loop the values 0, 1, and 2. Here we will use it for three short out-and-back moves and print the trial number so each movement can be identified in the output.

title: Lesson F5.1: Repeat a Known Count
heading: Worked example
text:
The body runs once for each value from `range(3)`. Adding one to `trial` prints 1, 2, and 3, while the two straight commands request an out-and-back move on each repeat.

~~~python
for trial in range(3):
    print("Trial:", trial + 1)
    robot.straight(100)
    robot.straight(-100)
~~~

title: Lesson F5.1: Repeat a Known Count
heading: Simulator practice
text: The starter repeats only an outward move. Add the reverse command and trial print from the worked example inside its loop. It should then show three out-and-back movements for `range(3)` and two for `range(2)`.

title: Lesson F5.1: Repeat a Known Count
heading: On the robot
text: The first physical test should have the wheels lifted so you can count the repeats. On the floor, a start mark can show whether each out-and-back movement returns to the same place.

title: Lesson F5.1: Repeat a Known Count
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The number of printed trials should match the number of completed moves. If it does not, check the `range()` value and which lines are indented under `for`.

Reference: [Pybricks first robot program](https://pybricks.com/learn/making-programs/your-first-program/).

title: Lesson F5.2: Repeat Until a Cue
heading: Overview
text: In F1.1 we used a line reading to stop a drive. A `while` loop makes that behavior possible because it checks the condition again after every pass. This lesson focuses on where the repeated reading happens and where the stop call belongs. If the line is missed, the loop will need a timeout, which we add later in this unit.

title: Lesson F5.2: Repeat Until a Cue
heading: Worked example
text:
`robot.drive(100, 0)` continues until another command stops it. Each pass through the loop waits 10 ms, then `color_sensor.reflection()` is checked again. When a reading is 35% or lower, Python leaves the loop and calls `robot.stop()`.

~~~python
robot.drive(100, 0)
while color_sensor.reflection() > 35:
    wait(10)
robot.stop()
~~~

title: Lesson F5.2: Repeat Until a Cue
heading: Simulator practice
text: Replace the starter's fixed-distance loop with the worked example's sensor loop. The simulator line should lower reflection enough to end it, and the field view can show where the sensor is at the stop. A real mat may need a different threshold.

title: Lesson F5.2: Repeat Until a Cue
heading: On the robot
text: The first physical trial should be slow and start near the line. Watching where the sensor and wheels are when the robot stops can show whether the threshold and speed suit the available space.

title: Lesson F5.2: Repeat Until a Cue
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The condition should be checked after each 10 ms wait, and `robot.stop()` should run after the loop ends. If the robot never detects the line, a timeout can bound the drive in the next lesson.

Reference: [Pybricks ColorSensor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/colorsensor.html).

title: Lesson F5.3: Wait and Measure Time
heading: Overview
text: We have used `wait(10)` to space sensor readings. `StopWatch.time()` gives us a way to measure how long a drive takes in milliseconds. In this lesson, the distance stays at 300 mm while we compare the time at two speeds. A long blocking wait would delay the next sensor check.

title: Lesson F5.3: Wait and Measure Time
heading: Worked example
text:
The watch starts before `robot.straight(300)`. The print line reports the elapsed time when that move finishes, and `wait(100)` then pauses for another 100 ms. Because the print comes first, its value does not include that final pause.

~~~python
watch = StopWatch()
robot.straight(300)
elapsed_ms = watch.time()
print("Elapsed ms:", elapsed_ms)
wait(100)
~~~

title: Lesson F5.3: Wait and Measure Time
heading: Simulator practice
text: Use the worked example in place of the starter's three short moves. The same 300 mm drive should take different simulated times at different straight speeds; keeping the distance fixed makes the time comparison clearer.

title: Lesson F5.3: Wait and Measure Time
heading: On the robot
text: Five physical run times with the battery state recorded beside each one may show a wider range than the simulator. The longest time can be a cautious number for match planning.

title: Lesson F5.3: Wait and Measure Time
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The printed time should describe the drive before the last 100 ms wait. Dividing it by 1000 gives seconds. If the number seems too large, check where the watch starts and which waits occur before the print.

Reference: [Pybricks timing tools reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/tools/).

title: Lesson F5.4: Add a Timeout
heading: Overview
text: A line stop needs a backup when the sensor never sees the line. A stopwatch can bound the wait so the drive ends after three seconds even if reflection stays above the threshold. The printed result should then tell us whether the line or the time limit ended the route.

title: Lesson F5.4: Add a Timeout
heading: Worked example
text:
The `while` condition requires both a light reading above 35% and elapsed time below 3000 ms. `robot.stop()` runs after either condition fails. The final `if` uses the watch to print which exit likely occurred.

~~~python
watch = StopWatch()
robot.drive(120, 0)
while color_sensor.reflection() > 35 and watch.time() < 3000:
    wait(10)
robot.stop()
if watch.time() >= 3000:
    print("Timed out")
else:
    print("Line found")
~~~

title: Lesson F5.4: Add a Timeout
heading: Simulator practice
text: Replace the starter's fixed-distance loop with the worked example. With the visible line, the sensor should end the drive first. A threshold below zero keeps the reflection condition true, so a second run should end on the timer.

title: Lesson F5.4: Add a Timeout
heading: On the robot
text: The first physical timeout test should use a clear practice surface and a person ready at the hub stop button. A timed stop there can show whether the backup works before the robot is sent toward a field model.

title: Lesson F5.4: Add a Timeout
heading: Check and adjust
text:
Both runs should reach `robot.stop()`, and the printed result should match the condition that ended each run. If the route lasts too long, check that the watch starts before the drive and that the loop compares its time.

Reference: [Pybricks timing tools reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/tools/).

title: Lesson F5.5: Loop and Timeout Challenge
heading: Overview
text: This challenge combines the loop, sensor readings, and timeout from the unit. The aim is an approach that can stop for a line, an obstacle, or a four-second limit and report the reason. The simulator checks that a loop reads reflected light or time, moves the robot, and calls `robot.stop()` without a collision.

title: Lesson F5.5: Loop and Timeout Challenge
heading: Worked example
text:
`reason` begins as `"timeout"`. A line or obstacle reading can replace it and break out of the loop. If neither condition is met, the watch ends the loop; the stop call is outside all three exit paths.

~~~python
watch = StopWatch()
reason = "timeout"
robot.drive(100, 0)
while watch.time() < 4000:
    if color_sensor.reflection() < 35:
        reason = "line"
        break
    if distance_sensor.distance() < 150:
        reason = "obstacle"
        break
    wait(10)
robot.stop()
print(reason)
~~~

title: Lesson F5.5: Loop and Timeout Challenge
heading: Simulator practice
text: The fixed field can support separate tests by changing a threshold or the time limit. Each test should print the reason expected for that setup and end with the robot stopped. Resetting between runs keeps the starting pose comparable.

title: Lesson F5.5: Loop and Timeout Challenge
heading: On the robot
text: Low-speed physical trials may show whether the three stop reasons correspond to different field positions. Marks or photos of those positions can help when choosing the final thresholds.

title: Lesson F5.5: Loop and Timeout Challenge
heading: Check and adjust
text:
Every loop exit should lead to `robot.stop()`. If a test keeps driving, check for a path that bypasses the stop and for a time condition that never becomes false.

Reference: [Pybricks timing tools reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/tools/).

title: Lesson F6.1: Define and Call Functions
heading: Overview
text: The route from the last unit can be grouped into named actions. A function's indented body runs only when the program calls it. Here we will define a short launch route and check what happens when the call is present or missing. The DriveBase should be created outside the function so each call uses the same robot settings.

title: Lesson F6.1: Define and Call Functions
heading: Worked example
text:
`leave_home()` contains a drive and a turn. Python stores that body at the `def` line, runs it at `leave_home()`, and then prints the completion message. Removing the call would leave the definition in place without moving the robot.

~~~python
def leave_home():
    robot.straight(250)
    robot.turn(90)

leave_home()
print("Launch route finished")
~~~

title: Lesson F6.1: Define and Call Functions
heading: Simulator practice
text: The starter already defines a simple drive function. Replacing it with `leave_home()` lets you compare a run with the call against one without it. The robot should move only when the function is called.

title: Lesson F6.1: Define and Call Functions
heading: On the robot
text: A named route function in Pybricks Code can help a teammate understand what a section of the program does. If its name and body disagree, the function may need a clearer name or a smaller job.

title: Lesson F6.1: Define and Call Functions
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The definition should describe the action, and the call should be the point where it happens. If the robot stays still after a definition, check for the call before changing the DriveBase code.

Reference: [Pybricks first robot program](https://pybricks.com/learn/making-programs/your-first-program/).

title: Lesson F6.2: Parameters and Return Values
heading: Overview
text: The function in the previous lesson always ran the same route. A parameter lets a call choose its distance, while `return` gives the caller a result. This lesson uses a distance parameter to move and a Boolean return value to report whether the color sensor sees the line at the end.

title: Lesson F6.2: Parameters and Return Values
heading: Worked example
text:
`approach_line(250)` passes 250 into `max_mm`. After driving, the function compares reflection with 35 and returns `True` or `False`. `line_found` stores that result; `return` itself does not move the robot.

~~~python
def approach_line(max_mm):
    robot.straight(max_mm)
    return color_sensor.reflection() < 35

line_found = approach_line(250)
print("Line found:", line_found)
~~~

title: Lesson F6.2: Parameters and Return Values
heading: Simulator practice
text: The simulator's line gives the return value something to test. A run with 250 mm and another with 350 mm may end at different sensor positions, so comparing `line_found` can show whether the endpoint affects the result.

title: Lesson F6.2: Parameters and Return Values
heading: On the robot
text: On the physical mat, a measured approach distance should leave room for the robot to stop safely. Three starts with that value can show whether the returned Boolean agrees with where the color sensor ends up.

title: Lesson F6.2: Parameters and Return Values
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The call's number should reach `max_mm`, and the returned Boolean should reach `line_found`. If every result is `False`, an endpoint reflection print may show whether the sensor ever reached the line.

Reference: [Pybricks ColorSensor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/colorsensor.html).

title: Lesson F6.3: Scope and Calibration Constants
heading: Overview
text: We can give a measured threshold one name and use it in more than one function. A variable created inside a function is local to that function, while a value defined above it can be read by both. Here `LINE_THRESHOLD` is the shared value and `light_percent` is the local reading.

title: Lesson F6.3: Scope and Calibration Constants
heading: Worked example
text:
`is_on_line()` reads reflection when called and compares it with `LINE_THRESHOLD`. The uppercase name signals a value the team intends to keep fixed during a run. A different measured threshold can be tried by changing that one definition.

~~~python
LINE_THRESHOLD = 35

def is_on_line():
    light_percent = color_sensor.reflection()
    return light_percent < LINE_THRESHOLD

print(is_on_line())
~~~

title: Lesson F6.3: Scope and Calibration Constants
heading: Simulator practice
text: The simulator starter prints a reflection reading. Put that reading in `is_on_line()`, then rerun with a different `LINE_THRESHOLD`. The changed Boolean can show that the function uses the named value.

title: Lesson F6.3: Scope and Calibration Constants
heading: On the robot
text: Physical light and dark readings may give a different threshold from the simulator's. Keeping those ranges beside the constant in the team's notes can show why that value was chosen.

title: Lesson F6.3: Scope and Calibration Constants
heading: Check and adjust
text:
Changing the shared constant should affect every call that reads it. If one call behaves differently, a second threshold literal or a local value may be hiding the intended constant.

Reference: [Pybricks ColorSensor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/colorsensor.html).

title: Lesson F6.4: Represent a Route with a List
heading: Overview
text: Several measured moves can be stored in a list instead of written as separate calls. Each pair in this lesson gives a straight distance in millimeters and then a turn in degrees. A loop can run the pairs in order, making the route table visible in one place.

title: Lesson F6.4: Represent a Route with a List
heading: Worked example
text:
The first pair requests a 300 mm drive and 90 degree turn. The second uses a negative turn, and the third skips turning because its angle is zero. Changing one pair should change one part of the route without rewriting the loop.

~~~python
route = [(300, 90), (50, -90), (150, 0)]
for distance_mm, turn_deg in route:
    robot.straight(distance_mm)
    if turn_deg != 0:
        robot.turn(turn_deg)
~~~

title: Lesson F6.4: Represent a Route with a List
heading: Simulator practice
text: The starter already uses a function for one drive. Replacing its route with the list above gives the simulator three drive segments to show. A change to the second pair should affect the middle segment and may change the final pose.

title: Lesson F6.4: Represent a Route with a List
heading: On the robot
text: A notebook table with distance and turn columns can help another teammate check the route. Physical measurements after each segment may show where the path first differs from that table.

title: Lesson F6.4: Represent a Route with a List
heading: Check and adjust
text:
Each route pair should cause one straight segment and, unless its angle is zero, one turn. If a segment looks wrong, check the pair's order and units before changing the loop.

Reference: [Pybricks DriveBase reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/robotics.html).

title: Lesson F6.5: Reusable Route Challenge
heading: Overview
text: This challenge uses one route function more than once. The simulator checks for a function definition, at least two calls to a route function, and movement without a collision. A return toward home gives those calls a route to describe, even though the check focuses on reuse and safe motion.

title: Lesson F6.5: Reusable Route Challenge
heading: Worked example
text:
`drive_and_turn()` takes a distance and a turn angle. Four calls request the sides and corners of a rectangle. If those distances and turns match the field, the path should finish near its starting point.

~~~python
def drive_and_turn(distance_mm, turn_deg):
    robot.straight(distance_mm)
    robot.turn(turn_deg)

drive_and_turn(300, 90)
drive_and_turn(50, 90)
drive_and_turn(300, 90)
drive_and_turn(50, 90)
~~~

title: Lesson F6.5: Reusable Route Challenge
heading: Simulator practice
text: The example gives the simulator a route that calls the same function four times. Changing one width in its call values may move the final position, which you can compare with a prediction from the route shape.

title: Lesson F6.5: Reusable Route Challenge
heading: On the robot
text: Three physical runs from the same launch mark can show how closely the rectangle closes. Recording each final position may help separate a repeated distance error from a turn that varies.

title: Lesson F6.5: Reusable Route Challenge
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The simulator should record a function definition, repeated calls, and motion without collision. On the mat, a rectangle that does not close may need its sides and turns measured separately.

Reference: [Pybricks DriveBase reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/robotics.html).

title: Lesson F7.1: Check Motor Direction
heading: Overview
text: Before choosing a tool angle, we need to know which way a positive command moves the attachment. `Motor` takes a configured positive direction, but gears and mounting may change the tool's visible direction. This lesson compares two settings with a small motor move so the sign can be recorded before a mission route uses it.

title: Lesson F7.1: Check Motor Direction
heading: Worked example
text:
The constructor sets the motor's positive direction to counterclockwise. `run_angle(150, 30)` requests a 30 degree move at 150 degrees per second, and `attachment.angle()` prints the motor's reported angle. The physical tool may move differently from that motor reading if gears reverse its output.

~~~python
attachment = Motor(Port.E, Direction.COUNTERCLOCKWISE)
attachment.run_angle(150, 30)
print("Tool angle:", attachment.angle())
~~~

title: Lesson F7.1: Check Motor Direction
heading: Simulator practice
text: The simulator starter moves the attachment with its default direction. Change the constructor to `Direction.COUNTERCLOCKWISE` and use the same positive 30 degree command. The visible arm should move the opposite way, while `attachment.angle()` still reports a positive motor angle. Comparing both runs helps establish which direction to use in later tool calls.

title: Lesson F7.1: Check Motor Direction
heading: On the robot
text: The real tool should have room to move during a small 30 degree test. A mark at its starting position can help show which direction a positive motor command actually moves the output.

title: Lesson F7.1: Check Motor Direction
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The recorded direction should let a teammate predict the next tool move. If the tool moves toward the frame instead of away from it, check the configured direction and gearing before using a larger angle.

Reference: [Pybricks Motor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/motor.html).

title: Lesson F7.2: Relative Tool Angles
heading: Overview
text: Now that a positive direction is known, we can use relative angles to move the tool out and back. `Motor.run_angle()` adds each requested rotation to the current motor position. A positive move followed by an equal negative move should bring the motor near its starting angle if the mechanism can complete both moves.

title: Lesson F7.2: Relative Tool Angles
heading: Worked example
text:
`start_deg` records the initial motor angle. The two `run_angle()` calls request 90 degrees out and 90 degrees back. The printed values can show whether the motor returned to its recorded start.

~~~python
start_deg = attachment.angle()
attachment.run_angle(180, 90)
print("After push:", attachment.angle())
attachment.run_angle(180, -90)
print("Back at:", attachment.angle(), "start:", start_deg)
~~~

title: Lesson F7.2: Relative Tool Angles
heading: Simulator practice
text: The simulator starter moves the attachment and prints its angle. Using the example's out-and-back pair should end near `start_deg`. Changing the first move to 60 degrees while leaving the return at 90 should produce a different final angle.

title: Lesson F7.2: Relative Tool Angles
heading: On the robot
text: Three physical out-and-back moves from a marked start may show whether the tool returns to the same place. A blocked mechanism can stop before the requested angle, so clearance matters as much as the printed motor value.

title: Lesson F7.2: Relative Tool Angles
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The motor reading should be close to its start after equal and opposite moves. If the physical tool is not, compare both printed angles and inspect the linkage for binding or slip.

Reference: [Pybricks Motor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/motor.html).

title: Lesson F7.3: Target Angles
heading: Overview
text: Relative angles add to the motor's current position. A target angle instead names a position to reach, which can be useful for an open or closed tool.
