This lesson sets a zero reference, moves to 90 degrees, and returns to zero. The reference should match a real physical position before the same numbers are used on a robot.

title: Lesson F7.3: Target Angles
heading: Worked example
text:
`attachment.reset_angle(OPEN_DEG)` labels the current motor position as zero. The two `run_target()` calls then request closed and open positions. If the tool was not actually open at the reset, the named positions would be misleading.

~~~python
OPEN_DEG = 0
CLOSED_DEG = 90
attachment.reset_angle(OPEN_DEG)
attachment.run_target(180, CLOSED_DEG)
attachment.run_target(180, OPEN_DEG)
~~~

title: Lesson F7.3: Target Angles
heading: Simulator practice
text: The simulator starter shows a relative move. Replacing it with the target calls above should move the tool to 90 degrees and back to zero. A different closed target can be tried after the visible travel is checked.

title: Lesson F7.3: Target Angles
heading: On the robot
text: The physical tool should be at a visible open reference when its angle is reset to zero. Tests without an object can show whether both target positions are clear before a light object is added.

title: Lesson F7.3: Target Angles
heading: Check and adjust
text:
Both targets should be reachable without forcing the mechanism. If the same number sends the tool to a different place on later runs, the zero reference or linkage may need checking.

Reference: [Pybricks Motor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/motor.html).

title: Lesson F7.4: Gearing, Load, and Stalls
heading: Overview
text: Gears can change how far the tool moves for one motor turn and how much torque reaches it. Pybricks can account for a known gear train through the Motor's `gears` setting. This lesson compares commanded angles with visible travel, then introduces a carefully limited way to find a physical home position. The simulator shows a simplified tool and cannot test binding.

title: Lesson F7.4: Gearing, Load, and Stalls
heading: Worked example
text:
The commented lines are for a physical mechanism after its safe travel has been checked. They show a gear list and a low duty limit for `run_until_stalled()` before resetting the angle. The active line is a measured 60 degree move that the simulator can show.

~~~python
attachment.run_angle(120, 60)
~~~

title: Lesson F7.4: Gearing, Load, and Stalls
heading: Simulator practice
text: The virtual attachment can show how a 60 degree command differs from 90 degrees. It should not be used to decide how much force a real attachment can safely take at a stop.

title: Lesson F7.4: Gearing, Load, and Stalls
heading: On the robot
text: The real gear train and output travel should be inspected with the robot off. If the hardware-only homing lines are used, the first test should be supervised with a low duty limit and a clear way to stop it.

title: Lesson F7.4: Gearing, Load, and Stalls
heading: Check and adjust
text:
A recorded safe angle range should come from physical tests, not the virtual tool. If the attachment binds during an ordinary move, inspect the gears and supports before relying on stall-based homing.

Reference: [Pybricks Motor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/motor.html).

title: Lesson F7.5: Attachment Control Challenge
heading: Overview
text: This challenge brings the drive and attachment together. The simulator checks for a tool move, an outward drive and return home, and no collision. We can use separate route and tool functions to see which part needs adjustment if the yellow target is missed.

title: Lesson F7.5: Attachment Control Challenge
heading: Worked example
text:
`activate_target()` requests a 300 mm approach and a 90 degree tool move followed by its return. The reverse drive requests a return toward home, and the print shows the final motor angle. The distance may need adjustment before the tool is close enough to touch the target.

~~~python
def activate_target():
    robot.straight(300)
    attachment.run_angle(150, 90)
    attachment.run_angle(150, -90)

activate_target()
robot.straight(-300)
print("Tool angle:", attachment.angle())
~~~

title: Lesson F7.5: Attachment Control Challenge
heading: Simulator practice
text: The yellow target gives the simulator a visible point to approach. A run should move the tool and return home without a collision. If the target stays inactive, the robot's approach position may be worth checking before the tool angle.

title: Lesson F7.5: Attachment Control Challenge
heading: On the robot
text: Five low-speed physical trials may show whether the robot reaches the target and whether the tool returns to its starting angle. Notes on contact, angle, and home position can separate navigation error from tool error.

title: Lesson F7.5: Attachment Control Challenge
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The simulator's required checks should pass, and the target can be inspected in the field view. If the target is missed on a real mat, compare approach position and tool travel before changing either value.

Reference: [Pybricks Motor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/motor.html).

title: Lesson F8.1: Wheel Diameter and Axle Track
heading: Overview
text: The DriveBase needs two measurements from the robot: wheel diameter and axle track. Diameter is measured across a wheel; axle track is the distance between the wheel contact points on the floor. We will use these values to compare a straight drive and a turn. The example numbers are starting values, so your own build should be measured before using them on hardware.

title: Lesson F8.1: Wheel Diameter and Axle Track
heading: Worked example
text:
Both measurements are in millimeters. A wrong diameter can affect the straight distance, while a wrong axle track can affect the turn angle.

~~~python
WHEEL_DIAMETER_MM = 56
AXLE_TRACK_MM = 112
robot = DriveBase(left_motor, right_motor,
                  wheel_diameter=WHEEL_DIAMETER_MM,
                  axle_track=AXLE_TRACK_MM)
robot.straight(500)
robot.turn(180)
~~~

title: Lesson F8.1: Wheel Diameter and Axle Track
heading: Simulator practice
text: Change the wheel diameter once and compare the reported distance and turn with the first run. This can help separate a geometry setting from a route command.

title: Lesson F8.1: Wheel Diameter and Axle Track
heading: On the robot
text: Measure the wheel and the contact-point spacing on the actual build. A 500 mm straight and a 180 degree turn from marked starts can show which measurement needs another look.

title: Lesson F8.1: Wheel Diameter and Axle Track
heading: Check and adjust
text:
Keep the two measurements and their separate errors on the calibration sheet. If straight distance is consistently wrong, check diameter first; a repeatable turn error may point to axle track.

Reference: [Pybricks DriveBase reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/robotics.html).

title: Lesson F8.2: Straight and Turn Segments
heading: Overview
text: A route can be built from short straight and turn segments. Each command finishes before the next starts, so we can compare the robot's position with a planned corner after every segment. A negative distance reverses, and a negative angle turns left. This lesson uses those signs to locate the first part of a route that misses.

title: Lesson F8.2: Straight and Turn Segments
heading: Worked example
text:
The reset gives the route a known distance and angle reading. The printed values describe the movement after the three segments, although they do not by themselves tell us whether the robot reached a field mark.

~~~python
robot.reset()
robot.straight(300)
robot.turn(90)
robot.straight(50)
print("Distance mm:", robot.distance())
print("Angle deg:", robot.angle())
~~~

title: Lesson F8.2: Straight and Turn Segments
heading: Simulator practice
text: Use the worked route to mark a predicted corner and endpoint, then step through it. The first mismatch is a better place to investigate than the final miss alone.

title: Lesson F8.2: Straight and Turn Segments
heading: On the robot
text: Tape marks at the corners can make the first error visible on the mat. Measure that error before adjusting the next segment.

title: Lesson F8.2: Straight and Turn Segments
heading: Check and adjust
text:
A route log should identify which segment first leaves the planned path. Retesting that segment on its own may show whether distance, turn angle, or launch pose caused the difference.

Reference: [Pybricks DriveBase reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/robotics.html).

title: Lesson F8.3: Arcs and Speed Settings
heading: Overview
text: An arc can round a corner that would otherwise need a straight segment and an in-place turn. `DriveBase.arc(radius, angle=...)` takes a radius in millimeters and an angle in degrees; a positive radius makes a right arc. We will compare two short arcs with a segmented route and watch the whole robot footprint, including its attachment.

title: Lesson F8.3: Arcs and Speed Settings
heading: Worked example
text:
The two arcs have equal radii with opposite signs. `settings()` also uses separate units for straight and turning motion: mm/s and mm/s², then deg/s and deg/s².

~~~python
robot.settings(160, 320, 90, 180)  # mm/s, mm/s², deg/s, deg/s²
robot.arc(100, angle=30)
robot.arc(-100, angle=30)
~~~

title: Lesson F8.3: Arcs and Speed Settings
heading: Simulator practice
text: Try the worked example's two arcs in the editor, then compare them with a route made from straight segments and in-place turns. The comparison can show whether the curve gives enough clearance on this field.

title: Lesson F8.3: Arcs and Speed Settings
heading: On the robot
text: A taped arc and the actual attachment can help reveal a clearance problem between the start and end points.

title: Lesson F8.3: Arcs and Speed Settings
heading: Check and adjust
text:
Record the radius and speed settings with their units. If the robot touches an obstacle during the arc, a wider radius or another route may leave more room.

Reference: [Pybricks DriveBase reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/robotics.html).

title: Lesson F8.4: Continuous Drive and Heading
heading: Overview
text: Unlike `straight()` and `turn()`, `DriveBase.drive(speed, turn_rate)` starts moving and lets the next line run immediately. The program therefore needs a condition that reaches `robot.stop()`. Here a stopwatch limits the drive to one second, and a heading reading can help us check the direction of the turn.

title: Lesson F8.4: Continuous Drive and Heading
heading: Worked example
text:
Speed is in millimeters per second; turn rate is in degrees per second. If DriveBase gyro control is enabled, `robot.reset()` is the appropriate way to reset its angle reference.

~~~python
robot.reset()
watch = StopWatch()
robot.drive(120, 15)
while watch.time() < 1000:
    wait(10)
robot.stop()
print("Heading deg:", hub.imu.heading())
~~~

title: Lesson F8.4: Continuous Drive and Heading
heading: Simulator practice
text: Put the timed drive from the worked example in the editor and predict the curve's direction. The stopped robot and printed heading can then be compared with that prediction.

title: Lesson F8.4: Continuous Drive and Heading
heading: On the robot
text: A clear area and reduced speed should be used for the first physical run. A floor mark can show whether the hub's heading agrees with the visible turn.

title: Lesson F8.4: Continuous Drive and Heading
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The run should end after about one second, with a heading sign consistent with the turn direction. If it keeps moving, inspect the loop condition and stop call before another attempt.

Reference: [Pybricks PrimeHub reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/hubs/primehub.html).

title: Lesson F8.5: Navigation Challenge
heading: Overview
text: This challenge brings measured straights and turns into one navigation route. The robot should cross the practice line, make two turns, and return home. Recording the landmarks along the way can show where a calibration profile changes the result; an arc can be considered after the segmented route works.

title: Lesson F8.5: Navigation Challenge
heading: Worked example
text:
The function follows the outgoing route in reverse to return. The final heading print gives one more observation, but home position and obstacle clearance still need to be checked in the field view.

~~~python
def cross_line_and_return():
    robot.straight(850)
    robot.turn(90)
    robot.straight(50)
    robot.straight(-50)
    robot.turn(-90)
    robot.straight(-850)

cross_line_and_return()
print("Heading:", hub.imu.heading())
~~~

title: Lesson F8.5: Navigation Challenge
heading: Simulator practice
text: Run from the fixed home pose and compare the line crossing, turns, and final position with the plan. The automatic profile table can reveal which landmark is missed first under a different calibration.

title: Lesson F8.5: Navigation Challenge
heading: On the robot
text: The tool should be installed while tracing the route on the mat. Marked corners and moderate speed can make a clearance or turn error easier to locate.

title: Lesson F8.5: Navigation Challenge
heading: Check and adjust
text:
A successful run should cross the line and return without a collision. For any profile that fails, record its first missed landmark before changing a later segment.

Reference: [Pybricks DriveBase reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/robotics.html).

title: Lesson F9.1: Calibrate Reflected Light
heading: Overview
text: Now that the robot can cross the practice line, we can measure how its sensor sees the mat and the dark surface. Several readings at the intended mounting height should show whether the ranges are separate enough for a threshold. A midpoint may be a useful first value, although line edges and lighting can change the readings.

title: Lesson F9.1: Calibrate Reflected Light
heading: Worked example
text:
The two lists come from positions before and after a drive. The candidate threshold is halfway between the lowest light sample and the highest dark sample, so it is useful only if the two ranges have a gap.

~~~python
light_samples = [color_sensor.reflection() for _ in range(5)]
robot.straight(750)
dark_samples = [color_sensor.reflection() for _ in range(5)]
print("Light:", light_samples, "Dark:", dark_samples)
threshold = (min(light_samples) + max(dark_samples)) / 2
print("Candidate:", threshold)
~~~

title: Lesson F9.1: Calibrate Reflected Light
heading: Simulator practice
text: Use the worked example to collect five readings at the fixed start and five more after the drive. The second set should come from the line; the drive distance may need adjusting if the sensor stops elsewhere.

title: Lesson F9.1: Calibrate Reflected Light
heading: On the robot
text: Collect five values on each surface with the real sensor mounted as it will be used. If the ranges do not overlap, a threshold between the highest dark and lowest light reading can be tested at the line edge.

title: Lesson F9.1: Calibrate Reflected Light
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The recorded ranges should show why a threshold was chosen. If they overlap, a mounting change or another set of readings may help before the stop code is used.

Reference: [Pybricks ColorSensor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/colorsensor.html).

title: Lesson F9.2: Stop at a Dark Line
heading: Overview
text: With a measured reflection threshold, the robot can stop when the sensor reaches a dark line. `DriveBase.drive()` keeps moving while the program checks `ColorSensor.reflection()`, so the loop should also have a timeout. We will compare two speeds to see how far the robot travels after detecting the line.

title: Lesson F9.2: Stop at a Dark Line
heading: Worked example
text:
The loop ends when reflection falls to 35 or below, or when three seconds pass. `robot.stop()` is reached after either outcome; the printed distance alone does not identify which condition ended the loop.

~~~python
watch = StopWatch()
robot.drive(100, 0)
while color_sensor.reflection() > 35 and watch.time() < 3000:
    wait(10)
robot.stop()
print("Stop mm:", robot.distance())
~~~

title: Lesson F9.2: Stop at a Dark Line
heading: Simulator practice
text: Use the worked example's timed line stop at 100 mm/s, then change the drive speed to 200 mm/s. The final distance and sensor position can show how speed affects the stop.

title: Lesson F9.2: Stop at a Dark Line
heading: On the robot
text: The gap between sensor and wheel contact point should be measured on the real build. Repeated stops at both speeds can show whether the robot needs a slower approach or an offset.

title: Lesson F9.2: Stop at a Dark Line
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The robot should stop whether it finds the line or reaches the time limit. If it passes the desired mark, reducing speed or allowing for sensor position may improve the result.

Reference: [Pybricks ColorSensor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/colorsensor.html).

title: Lesson F9.3: Classify a Field Color
heading: Overview
text: Reflected light gives a number, while `ColorSensor.color()` gives a Pybricks Color label. A large colored target may be easier to identify by label. This lesson compares labels at two field positions, then asks whether the same label is dependable on the actual mission model.

title: Lesson F9.3: Classify a Field Color
heading: Worked example
text:
The program prints the current label and gives a message only when it is green. It does not move the robot to a colored area; that route is part of the practice.

~~~python
from pybricks.parameters import Color

seen = color_sensor.color()
print("Color:", seen)
if seen == Color.GREEN:
    print("Delivery zone")
~~~

title: Lesson F9.3: Classify a Field Color
heading: Simulator practice
text: Start with the worked example to print a label at the fixed start, then add a short route to the colored zone and print again. Comparing both readings can show whether the sensor reached the intended surface.

title: Lesson F9.3: Classify a Field Color
heading: On the robot
text: On the real robot, labels should be collected at the intended sensor height. Moving a few millimeters and repeating the reading can reveal a sensitive edge or uneven target.

title: Lesson F9.3: Classify a Field Color
heading: Check and adjust
text:
Record which labels remain consistent across nearby positions. If a label changes easily, reflected light or a larger target may be more useful for that mission.

Reference: [Pybricks ColorSensor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/colorsensor.html).

title: Lesson F9.4: Follow an Edge Briefly
heading: Overview
text: A line follower can steer toward an edge by comparing current reflection with a target value. The difference, called an error, changes the turn rate each time the loop runs. Here we will test the direction of that correction at low speed for a short interval. The simulator's short line supports a steering demonstration, not a long route.

title: Lesson F9.4: Follow an Edge Briefly
heading: Worked example
text:
The sign of `error * 0.5` determines which way the robot turns. A single sensor can lose track of which side of the line it is on after it leaves the edge entirely.

~~~python
target = 35
watch = StopWatch()
while watch.time() < 300:
    error = color_sensor.reflection() - target
    robot.drive(40, error * 0.5)
    wait(20)
robot.stop()
~~~

title: Lesson F9.4: Follow an Edge Briefly
heading: Simulator practice
text: Try the worked example's 300 ms steering loop, then reverse the correction sign and compare the headings. The result can show which direction moves the sensor toward the edge.

title: Lesson F9.4: Follow an Edge Briefly
heading: On the robot
text: A wide practice line and clear space should be used for the first physical test. Record whether the sensor stays near the intended edge for the brief run.

title: Lesson F9.4: Follow an Edge Briefly
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The timer should stop the drive after the short test. If the correction steers away from the chosen edge, its sign may need reversing before a longer attempt.

Reference: [Pybricks ColorSensor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/colorsensor.html).

title: Lesson F9.5: Sensor Route Challenge
heading: Overview
text: This challenge uses a sensor reading to end a drive, with a timeout for a missed line. The goal is to stop at the dark line, then test what happens when the threshold cannot be reached. The two outcomes should both leave the robot stopped before the next field object.

title: Lesson F9.5: Sensor Route Challenge
heading: Worked example
text:
The first straight drive puts the sensor nearer the line. The continuous drive then ends on a dark reading or after eight seconds. The example prints the final reflection, and the elapsed time can also be printed to distinguish the two outcomes.

~~~python
robot.straight(200)
watch = StopWatch()
robot.drive(90, 0)
while color_sensor.reflection() > 35 and watch.time() < 8000:
    wait(10)
robot.stop()
print("Light:", color_sensor.reflection())
~~~

title: Lesson F9.5: Sensor Route Challenge
heading: Simulator practice
text: Use the sample route for a first line stop. Changing its threshold to a value below zero should force the timeout path; compare the final position and stop event after both runs.

title: Lesson F9.5: Sensor Route Challenge
heading: On the robot
text: Five physical starts from the same launch mark can show how much the stop distance varies. Record any run that misses the line as well as the successful ones.

title: Lesson F9.5: Sensor Route Challenge
heading: Check and adjust
text:
Both runs should end with a stopped drive base. If the line is missed, the reading and elapsed time can help determine whether the threshold or the route needs adjustment.

Reference: [Pybricks ColorSensor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/colorsensor.html).

title: Lesson F10.1: Read Ultrasonic Range
heading: Overview
text: An ultrasonic reading can help the robot judge how far it is from an object. `UltrasonicSensor.distance()` reports millimeters, with 2000 indicating that no valid distance was measured in the current Pybricks API. We will compare readings at two positions and keep an invalid reading separate from a clear path.

title: Lesson F10.1: Read Ultrasonic Range
heading: Worked example
text:
The conditional prints either an invalid-range message or a measured distance. A narrow or angled target may give a poor echo, so one reading should not decide a close approach.

~~~python
range_mm = distance_sensor.distance()
if range_mm == 2000:
    print("No valid range")
else:
    print("Range mm:", range_mm)
~~~

title: Lesson F10.1: Read Ultrasonic Range
heading: Simulator practice
text: The starter already prints an initial range. Add a short approach and another range print. Different route distances can show how the number changes near the fixed obstacle.

title: Lesson F10.1: Read Ultrasonic Range
heading: On the robot
text: A ruler can provide a comparison for the sensor on hardware. Flat and angled targets may produce different results at the same physical gap.

title: Lesson F10.1: Read Ultrasonic Range
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The log should distinguish a valid distance from 2000, which means the measurement was unavailable. If invalid readings recur, the target's angle and surface are useful things to check.

Reference: [Pybricks UltrasonicSensor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/ultrasonicsensor.html).

title: Lesson F10.2: Use a Force Sensor
heading: Overview
text: A Force Sensor can report whether a bumper or tool has pressed against an object. In the simulator, contact is estimated from position and tool angle; on a robot, `ForceSensor.pressed()` tests a minimum force in newtons. This lesson compares the simulated contact cue with the hardware setup needed to measure real contact.

title: Lesson F10.2: Use a Force Sensor
heading: Worked example
text:
Port F is only an example assignment. The force threshold and mounting should match the physical bumper, which needs room to move before rigid parts meet the model.

~~~python
from pybricks.pupdevices import ForceSensor
bumper = ForceSensor(Port.F)
print("Contact:", bumper.pressed(force=3))
~~~

title: Lesson F10.2: Use a Force Sensor
heading: Simulator practice
text: Use the worked example's force reading at the start, then add a route toward the yellow target and a 60 degree tool move before reading again. A changed value would indicate simulated contact under this approximate model.

title: Lesson F10.2: Use a Force Sensor
heading: On the robot
text: With a real sensor on the configured port, hand presses should show both released and pressed results before a slow approach is attempted.

title: Lesson F10.2: Use a Force Sensor
heading: Check and adjust
text:
Record the actual force and tool position when contact occurs on hardware. The simulator's contact estimate can suggest a route, but the real bumper determines the usable threshold.

Reference: [Pybricks ForceSensor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/forcesensor.html).

title: Lesson F10.3: Read and Reset Heading
heading: Overview
text: Heading gives the robot a way to check its turn against a reference direction. `PrimeHub.imu.heading()` reports clockwise positive degrees relative to the program start or last reset. This lesson resets the reference through DriveBase, makes a turn, and compares the reported heading with a floor mark.

title: Lesson F10.3: Read and Reset Heading
heading: Worked example
text:
The drive base is stopped before `robot.reset(angle=0)`. With DriveBase gyro control, a direct IMU reset during driving can raise an error in current Pybricks.

~~~python
robot.stop()
robot.reset(angle=0)
robot.turn(90)
heading_deg = hub.imu.heading()
print("Heading deg:", heading_deg)
~~~

title: Lesson F10.3: Read and Reset Heading
heading: Simulator practice
text: Try the worked example's right turn from reset, then change the angle for a left turn. The signs and magnitudes can be compared with the commanded turns.

title: Lesson F10.3: Read and Reset Heading
heading: On the robot
text: Let the real robot settle before reading the heading. Three trials against a marked 90 degree floor angle can show whether the turn is consistent.

title: Lesson F10.3: Read and Reset Heading
heading: Check and adjust
text:
Record the commanded angle, measured heading, and difference for each trial. A repeated difference may point to turn calibration; a varying one may need a closer look at grip or launch position.

Reference: [Pybricks PrimeHub reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/hubs/primehub.html).

title: Lesson F10.4: Handle Missing or Conflicting Cues
heading: Overview
text: A missing sensor reading needs a defined outcome in a mission program. Here the robot waits briefly for a valid ultrasonic distance. It moves only when the reading is valid and leaves enough room; otherwise it stops. This makes the decision visible in the printed result.

title: Lesson F10.4: Handle Missing or Conflicting Cues
heading: Worked example
text:
The `valid` flag begins false and changes only after a reading below 2000. The one-second limit prevents the polling loop from waiting indefinitely.

~~~python
watch = StopWatch()
valid = False
while watch.time() < 1000:
    range_mm = distance_sensor.distance()
    if range_mm < 2000:
        valid = True
        break
    wait(20)
if valid and range_mm > 150:
    robot.straight(100)
else:
    robot.stop()
print("Valid range:", valid)
~~~

title: Lesson F10.4: Handle Missing or Conflicting Cues
heading: Simulator practice
text: Start with the worked example's `valid` check. Temporary sample values of 100 and 2000 mm can exercise both branches before the fixed-field reading is used; the printed flag can show which branch ran.

title: Lesson F10.4: Handle Missing or Conflicting Cues
heading: On the robot
text: The physical test should begin at low speed in clear space. If invalid readings are common, the team can decide whether this mission should be skipped or approached another way.

title: Lesson F10.4: Handle Missing or Conflicting Cues
heading: Check and adjust
text:
An invalid reading should leave the drive base stopped and print `False`. If it moves, inspect where the `valid` flag changes and which branch uses it.

Reference: [Pybricks UltrasonicSensor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/ultrasonicsensor.html).

title: Lesson F10.5: Sensor Check Challenge
heading: Overview
text: This challenge combines range and heading in a short approach. The robot should stop before contact and report where it is facing. A timeout gives the approach an end even if the target cannot be measured, while actual clearance still needs to be checked on hardware.

title: Lesson F10.5: Sensor Check Challenge
heading: Worked example
text:
The loop stops when the range is below 150 mm, becomes invalid at 2000, or reaches three seconds. The example does not require a valid first reading before motion begins, so that stricter behavior would need an initial range check.

~~~python
watch = StopWatch()
robot.drive(80, 0)
while watch.time() < 3000:
    range_mm = distance_sensor.distance()
    if range_mm < 150 or range_mm == 2000:
        break
    wait(10)
robot.stop()
print("Range mm:", range_mm)
print("Heading deg:", hub.imu.heading())
~~~

title: Lesson F10.5: Sensor Check Challenge
heading: Simulator practice
text: Try the sample approach on the fixed field, then change its threshold or initial heading. A short timeout can exercise the missing-cue case; every run should end with a stop event.

title: Lesson F10.5: Sensor Check Challenge
heading: On the robot
text: Reduced speed should be used for the physical approach. Measure the clearance after each stop to see whether the threshold leaves enough room for the real robot.

title: Lesson F10.5: Sensor Check Challenge
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The final log should include both range and heading. If the target is absent, the loop should still exit within three seconds and leave the drive base stopped.

Reference: [Pybricks UltrasonicSensor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/ultrasonicsensor.html).

title: Lesson F11.1: Break a Mission into Actions
heading: Overview
text: A complete mission has several parts: leaving home, approaching a model, acting, checking the result, and returning. We can give each part a function so a missed target can be traced to a smaller piece of the route. This lesson starts with an approach, a tool action, and a return.

title: Lesson F11.1: Break a Mission into Actions
heading: Worked example
text:
The distance is passed to both movement functions, so the return is the same length as the approach. A real mission may need a different return path if the outgoing path is blocked.

~~~python
def approach_target(distance_mm):
    robot.straight(distance_mm)

def activate():
    attachment.run_angle(180, 90)
    attachment.run_angle(180, -90)

def return_home(distance_mm):
    robot.straight(-distance_mm)

approach_target(300)
activate()
return_home(300)
~~~

title: Lesson F11.1: Break a Mission into Actions
heading: Simulator practice
text: Put the worked example's functions in the editor, then run each from a known pose before combining them. The first function that misses its planned position can then be adjusted without changing the others.

title: Lesson F11.1: Break a Mission into Actions
heading: On the robot
text: A route diagram with the function names can help a teammate connect code to field positions. Testing one function from a marked start may reveal an assumption about launch alignment.

title: Lesson F11.1: Break a Mission into Actions
heading: Check and adjust
text:
For each function, record where the robot should start and what visible result should follow. If the full route fails, the first mismatching result gives a focused place to retest.

Reference: [Pybricks first robot program](https://pybricks.com/learn/making-programs/your-first-program/).

title: Lesson F11.2: Plan Attachment Clearance
heading: Overview
text: An attachment changes the space the robot needs along a route. Even if the chassis clears an obstacle, the tool may reach into it while opening or closing. This lesson uses a named clearance distance for the approach, then checks the tool's full sweep around the target.

title: Lesson F11.2: Plan Attachment Clearance
heading: Worked example
text:
The approach stops short by `TOOL_CLEARANCE_MM` before the tool moves. The number is an example; the real margin should come from the attachment's reach and a field measurement.

~~~python
TOOL_CLEARANCE_MM = 70
target_gap_mm = 400
approach_mm = target_gap_mm - TOOL_CLEARANCE_MM
robot.straight(approach_mm)
attachment.run_angle(160, 60)
~~~

title: Lesson F11.2: Plan Attachment Clearance
heading: Simulator practice
text: Use the worked example's clearance value for a first approach, then compare the tool at each end of its travel. The field view can show whether the approach leaves room near the yellow target.

title: Lesson F11.2: Plan Attachment Clearance
heading: On the robot
text: Tracing the widest tool position on paper can help estimate its swept space. A slow physical test should then measure the closest gap with the actual tool installed.

title: Lesson F11.2: Plan Attachment Clearance
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The gap should remain positive through the whole tool motion. If contact occurs, measuring the full sweep can show whether the margin or route needs changing.

Reference: [Pybricks Motor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/motor.html).

title: Lesson F11.3: Choose a Mission Program
heading: Overview
text: When a match uses more than one launch, the team needs a reliable way to choose the intended mission. The simulator can use a mission name variable; Pybricks Code provides five Prime Hub program slots. We will compare named routes and connect each physical slot with a launch mark and attachment.

title: Lesson F11.3: Choose a Mission Program
heading: Worked example
text:
The `if` and `elif` branches run different routes for two known names. Any other name prints a message, and the final stop call still runs.

~~~python
MISSION = "target"

if MISSION == "target":
    robot.straight(300)
    attachment.run_angle(160, 60)
elif MISSION == "line":
    robot.straight(700)
else:
    print("Unknown mission")
robot.stop()
~~~

title: Lesson F11.3: Choose a Mission Program
heading: Simulator practice
text: Use the worked example's `MISSION` branches, changing the name to each known value and then an unknown one. The printed message and robot motion should make the selected branch clear.

title: Lesson F11.3: Choose a Mission Program
heading: On the robot
text: Two small programs can be saved in separate hub slots. A table linking each slot to its attachment and launch mark can help the team choose correctly at the field.

title: Lesson F11.3: Choose a Mission Program
heading: Check and adjust
text:
A teammate should be able to choose the intended route from the slot labels and launch plan. If another route runs, check the selected slot or mission name before changing movement values.

Reference: [Pybricks program guide](https://pybricks.com/learn/getting-started/pybricks-environment/).

title: Lesson F11.4: Coordinate Drive and Tool Motion
heading: Overview
text: Once a drive and tool action work in sequence, some robots can perform them at the same time. That may shorten a route, but the tool needs clearance along the whole drive. Here the simulator shows the sequential actions; the hardware-only `wait=False` option introduces overlap after the route has been checked.

title: Lesson F11.4: Coordinate Drive and Tool Motion
heading: Worked example
text:
The first part is suitable for the simulator. The commented lines show how Pybricks can start a tool move without waiting and later check whether it is done. The simulator does not model that concurrent timing.

~~~python
robot.straight(250)
attachment.run_angle(180, 60)
robot.straight(150)
print("Tool done:", attachment.done())

~~~

title: Lesson F11.4: Coordinate Drive and Tool Motion
heading: Simulator practice
text: Use the sequential route from the worked example and note its time and clearance. That baseline can be compared with a later physical test of overlapping motion.

title: Lesson F11.4: Coordinate Drive and Tool Motion
heading: On the robot
text: The hardware-only option should first be checked with the robot raised. A later low-speed field trial can show whether it saves time without bringing the tool into an obstacle.

title: Lesson F11.4: Coordinate Drive and Tool Motion
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The overlapping route is useful only if the tool clears the models and its measured time improves. A collision or uncertain clearance is a reason to use the tested sequential version.

Reference: [Pybricks Motor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/motor.html).

title: Lesson F11.5: Mission Cycle Challenge
heading: Overview
text: This challenge combines a target action, a delivery, and a return in one cycle. Separate functions can make the route easier to test, while time readings can show which action takes the longest. The worked example covers a target action and return, so the delivery step still needs to be planned and added.

title: Lesson F11.5: Mission Cycle Challenge
heading: Worked example
text:
The stopwatch measures from the start of the program. `target_step()` moves the attachment, and `return_step()` goes back after a half turn; neither function verifies that an object was delivered.

~~~python
watch = StopWatch()

def target_step():
    robot.straight(300)
    attachment.run_angle(180, 90)
    attachment.run_angle(180, -90)

def return_step():
    robot.turn(180)
    robot.straight(300)

target_step()
print("Target ms:", watch.time())
return_step()
print("Total ms:", watch.time())
~~~

title: Lesson F11.5: Mission Cycle Challenge
heading: Simulator practice
text: Add a delivery step for the generic field, then compare target, delivery, and home results over three attempts. The total time can be recorded alongside each result.

title: Lesson F11.5: Mission Cycle Challenge
heading: On the robot
text: The physical route should use the actual tool. A marked point for a short return can help if the pickup fails before delivery.

title: Lesson F11.5: Mission Cycle Challenge
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The completed route should attempt both objectives and end at home within the time budget. If it misses, separate trials may reveal which action first changed the planned pose.

Reference: [FIRST season materials](https://www.firstinspires.org/resources/library/fll/season-materials).

title: Lesson F12.1: Record Repeatability
heading: Overview
text: A single successful run does not show how often a route works. Repeating the same program from the same launch marks can reveal variation in final position, heading, time, and mission result. This lesson introduces a mean and a spread for time, then uses a table to keep all outcomes visible.

title: Lesson F12.1: Record Repeatability
heading: Worked example
text:
The mean describes the center of these three times. The spread is the longest minus the shortest, so a large spread may point to inconsistent starts or motion.

~~~python
times_ms = [3200, 3350, 3280]
mean_ms = sum(times_ms) / len(times_ms)
spread_ms = max(times_ms) - min(times_ms)
print("Mean ms:", mean_ms)
print("Spread ms:", spread_ms)
~~~

title: Lesson F12.1: Record Repeatability
heading: Simulator practice
text: The starter provides a fixed drive for the automatic three-profile table. Those profiles represent different calibrations, so their results should be recorded separately from repeated physical trials.

title: Lesson F12.1: Record Repeatability
heading: On the robot
text: Five physical trials from the same launch marks can show how much the actual result varies. Include failed runs and their endpoints in the table.

title: Lesson F12.1: Record Repeatability
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The table should make the spread and any consistent error visible. If results vary widely, launch alignment and loose hardware are useful checks before changing a calibration number.

Reference: [Pybricks timing tools reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/tools/).

title: Lesson F12.2: Calibrate Wheel Diameter
heading: Overview
text: After recording repeatable straight-drive errors, we can estimate a better wheel diameter. A robot that consistently stops short may need a smaller configured diameter; one that travels too far may need a larger one. The estimate uses the old diameter multiplied by actual distance and divided by requested distance.

title: Lesson F12.2: Calibrate Wheel Diameter
heading: Worked example
text:
The example turns a 480 mm measured drive for a 500 mm request into a new starting value. Axle track stays fixed during this pass so its effect is easier to separate.

~~~python
old_diameter_mm = 56
requested_mm = 500
actual_mm = 480
new_diameter_mm = old_diameter_mm * actual_mm / requested_mm
print("Try wheel diameter mm:", new_diameter_mm)
~~~

title: Lesson F12.2: Calibrate Wheel Diameter
heading: Simulator practice
text: Try the calculated diameter in code and rerun the 500 mm drive. The automatic profile table can show whether the adjustment improves distance across different calibrations.

title: Lesson F12.2: Calibrate Wheel Diameter
heading: On the robot
text: At least three measured 500 mm drives can show whether the error is consistent. After trying the estimate on the real robot, another set of measurements should confirm the change.

title: Lesson F12.2: Calibrate Wheel Diameter
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The chosen value should reduce the repeated straight error. If the estimate makes it worse, check which distance was actual and which was requested before adjusting again.

Reference: [Pybricks DriveBase reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/robotics.html).

title: Lesson F12.3: Calibrate Axle Track
heading: Overview
text: Once straight travel is calibrated, a full turn can help estimate axle track. Pybricks recommends a 360 degree turn on a clear surface. If the robot repeatedly turns too far, a smaller configured track may help; a short turn may call for a larger one.

title: Lesson F12.3: Calibrate Axle Track
heading: Worked example
text:
The example uses a 375 degree actual turn for a 360 degree request to calculate a smaller starting track. A single turn is an estimate, so the result still needs repeated checks.

~~~python
old_track_mm = 112
requested_deg = 360
actual_deg = 375
new_track_mm = old_track_mm * requested_deg / actual_deg
print("Try axle track mm:", new_track_mm)
~~~

title: Lesson F12.3: Calibrate Axle Track
heading: Simulator practice
text: Replace the starter's straight drive with a 360 degree turn and compare headings in the automatic profile table. After changing axle track in code, the same route can show whether the difference shrinks.

title: Lesson F12.3: Calibrate Axle Track
heading: On the robot
text: Three full turns from the same floor mark may show whether the error repeats. Small track adjustments can then be checked against both turns and straight distance.

title: Lesson F12.3: Calibrate Axle Track
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The selected track should improve the turns without undoing the straight calibration. If results vary between trials, grip and chassis structure may need attention before another numerical change.

Reference: [Pybricks DriveBase reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/robotics.html).

title: Lesson F12.4: Recover from a Failed Cue
heading: Overview
text: A mission may need a different route when a sensor cue is missed. Here the approach function returns `True` only if the dark line is detected before the timeout. The tool action depends on that result; otherwise the robot takes a short return path.

title: Lesson F12.4: Recover from a Failed Cue
heading: Worked example
text:
The function stops the drive before returning its Boolean. The reverse distance in the `else` branch is an example and should be checked against the actual path home.

~~~python
def approach_with_timeout():
    watch = StopWatch()
    robot.drive(90, 0)
    while color_sensor.reflection() > 35 and watch.time() < 2500:
        wait(10)
    robot.stop()
    return color_sensor.reflection() <= 35

if approach_with_timeout():
    attachment.run_angle(160, 60)
else:
    print("Skip tool action")
    robot.straight(-150)
~~~

title: Lesson F12.4: Recover from a Failed Cue
heading: Simulator practice
text: Use the worked example's approach and return branches. Setting its threshold below zero should force the failed-cue branch; compare that run with the measured threshold and check whether the attachment moves only after a detected line.

title: Lesson F12.4: Recover from a Failed Cue
heading: On the robot
text: The physical failed-cue test should begin from a safe launch. Its reverse path needs enough clearance for the actual tool, even when the line is missed.

title: Lesson F12.4: Recover from a Failed Cue
heading: Check and adjust
text:
A missed line should leave the tool still and lead to the planned return. If the tool moves, the returned value and its `if` condition are the first places to inspect.

Reference: [Pybricks ColorSensor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/colorsensor.html).

title: Lesson F12.5: Reliability Challenge
heading: Overview
text: This challenge asks whether one route can cross the dark line and return home under the simulator's three calibration profiles. The profile table can reveal how sensitive the route is to changed geometry or motion. A failed profile gives us a place to measure before adjusting the program.

title: Lesson F12.5: Reliability Challenge
heading: Worked example
text:
The sample route crosses the line, turns around, and drives the same nominal distance back. The final heading helps check the turn, while the field view shows whether the robot actually reached home.

~~~python
def short_route():
    robot.straight(850)
    robot.turn(180)
    robot.straight(850)

short_route()
print("Final heading:", hub.imu.heading())
~~~

title: Lesson F12.5: Reliability Challenge
heading: Simulator practice
text: Run once and record success, endpoint, heading, and time for each automatic profile. Keeping that baseline makes a later adjustment easier to judge.

title: Lesson F12.5: Reliability Challenge
heading: On the robot
text: Five physical trials with the same program and launch pose can show whether the simulator's sensitivity appears on the real robot. Record both successes and the first failure point.

title: Lesson F12.5: Reliability Challenge
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The log should support a claim about the route's repeatability. If one profile fails, locate its first divergence and rerun all three profiles after a measured change.

Reference: [Pybricks DriveBase reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/robotics.html).

title: Lesson F13.1: Compare Mission Value
heading: Overview
text: Mission points are only part of a match plan. A route that scores often may contribute more than a higher-value route that rarely succeeds. This lesson uses trial results to estimate expected points, then compares that estimate with the time a mission takes.

title: Lesson F13.1: Compare Mission Value
heading: Worked example
text:
Four successes in five trials give an estimated success rate of 0.8. Multiplying by the example's 20 points gives a simple expected value; it does not include how this mission affects another route.

~~~python
points = 20
successes = 4
trials = 5
success_rate = successes / trials
expected_points = points * success_rate
print("Expected points:", expected_points)
~~~

title: Lesson F13.1: Compare Mission Value
heading: Simulator practice
text: Replace the starter's route with the worked calculation, then use two sets of practice points and trial counts to compare expected values. The simulator's generic score should not be treated as an official season score.

title: Lesson F13.1: Compare Mission Value
heading: On the robot
text: The team's real trial counts and current Robot Game values can replace the examples. Attachment changes and route time may change which mission fits best.

title: Lesson F13.1: Compare Mission Value
heading: Check and adjust
text:
A useful comparison should show points, trial counts, estimated success rate, and time for both options. Few trials may leave the estimate uncertain, even when the calculated value looks high.

Reference: [FIRST season materials](https://www.firstinspires.org/resources/library/fll/season-materials).

title: Lesson F13.2: Budget the Match
heading: Overview
text: The match clock includes handling at home as well as driving and tool motion. We can add those times to see whether a planned set of missions fits within 150 seconds. A reserve for recovery gives the team room when a launch takes longer than expected.

title: Lesson F13.2: Budget the Match
heading: Worked example
text:
The list contains three mission estimates in seconds. Five seconds is added for each launch, followed by a 15 second reserve; the final Boolean reports whether the total fits.

~~~python
mission_times_s = [32, 41, 28]
launch_s = 5 * len(mission_times_s)
reserve_s = 15
planned_s = sum(mission_times_s) + launch_s + reserve_s
print("Planned seconds:", planned_s)
print("Fits match:", planned_s <= 150)
~~~

title: Lesson F13.2: Budget the Match
heading: Simulator practice
text: Use the worked calculation in the editor and replace its mission estimates with measured times. If a stopwatch reports milliseconds, divide by 1000 before adding them to this seconds-based plan.

title: Lesson F13.2: Budget the Match
heading: On the robot
text: Physical timing should include program selection, alignment, and attachment handling. The longest recent complete run may be a more useful planning number than the fastest one.

title: Lesson F13.2: Budget the Match
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The plan should fit inside 150 seconds with its reserve stated. If it does not, shortening a route or removing an objective may be more realistic than using only best-case times.

Reference: [Pybricks timing tools reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/tools/).

title: Lesson F13.3: Order Missions
heading: Overview
text: Changing mission order can change travel time, attachment handling, and the return path after a failure. This lesson compares two orders using measured time and a clear launch plan. The order should also leave a safe return if an uncertain action does not work.

title: Lesson F13.3: Order Missions
heading: Worked example
text:
The list prints a proposed sequence and launch number. It does not execute the missions, so the simulator practice needs routes for the selected order.

~~~python
mission_order = ["line", "target", "delivery"]
for launch_number, mission in enumerate(mission_order, start=1):
    print("Launch", launch_number, mission)
~~~

title: Lesson F13.3: Order Missions
heading: Simulator practice
text: The worked list only prints an order. Turn it into route calls before comparing two sequences on the practice field; total time and ending position can show differences that the list alone cannot.

title: Lesson F13.3: Order Missions
heading: On the robot
text: Attachments can be laid out in launch order for a physical rehearsal. The people who will run the match can time the handoff between programs.

title: Lesson F13.3: Order Missions
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The written plan should connect each launch to a program, attachment, mark, expected time, and return route. A second launch needs a known starting pose before its timing is meaningful.

Reference: [FIRST season materials](https://www.firstinspires.org/resources/library/fll/season-materials).

title: Lesson F13.4: Plan a Skip Decision
heading: Overview
text: A match plan can include a choice for limited time or a missed cue. Here a condition checks both time remaining and whether the target is ready. The printed choice represents a decision the team can rehearse before using it with real route functions.

title: Lesson F13.4: Plan a Skip Decision
heading: Worked example
text:
With 38 seconds left but `target_ready` false, the example chooses the short return. Both conditions must be true before it prints the target mission.

~~~python
time_left_s = 38
target_ready = False
if time_left_s >= 30 and target_ready:
    print("Run target mission")
else:
    print("Run short return mission")
~~~

title: Lesson F13.4: Plan a Skip Decision
heading: Simulator practice
text: Try the worked condition with three time values and both target states. The six printed outcomes can show whether it matches the team's written rule.

title: Lesson F13.4: Plan a Skip Decision
heading: On the robot
text: The same rule can be rehearsed with a stopwatch and the physical hub slots. Switching programs takes time that should appear in the match budget.

title: Lesson F13.4: Plan a Skip Decision
heading: Check and adjust
text:
A teammate should be able to choose the planned route from the rule without reading source code. If the choice takes too long, the slot labels or handling plan may need simplifying.

Reference: [Pybricks timing tools reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/tools/).

title: Lesson F13.5: Match Plan Challenge
heading: Overview
text: This challenge brings mission value, timing, order, and fallback into one plan. The team should be able to explain why the first route comes first and how much time remains for the next objective and return. Three complete trials can show whether that plan fits the clock in practice.

title: Lesson F13.5: Match Plan Challenge
heading: Worked example
text:
The example times two route functions and prints a reading after each. It models movement in one continuous simulator program; physical launches also include handling and may use separate hub slots.

~~~python
watch = StopWatch()

def launch_one():
    robot.straight(1380)
    attachment.run_angle(160, 90)
    attachment.run_angle(160, -90)
    robot.turn(180)
    robot.straight(1380)
    robot.turn(180)

def launch_two():
    robot.straight(850)
    robot.turn(180)
    robot.straight(850)

launch_one()
print("After one ms:", watch.time())
launch_two()
print("Total ms:", watch.time())
~~~

title: Lesson F13.5: Match Plan Challenge
heading: Simulator practice
text: Run the sequence under the 150 second clock. Record whether each objective was completed, where the robot ended, and how much time the route used.

title: Lesson F13.5: Match Plan Challenge
heading: On the robot
text: Physical rehearsal should include every handoff between launches. Comparing the total with the planned reserve can reveal time missing from the code-only estimate.

title: Lesson F13.5: Match Plan Challenge
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The final plan should include route order, time estimates, a fallback, and results from three complete trials. A run that uses the reserve may call for a shorter second objective.

Reference: [FIRST season materials](https://www.firstinspires.org/resources/library/fll/season-materials).

title: Lesson F14.1: Organize the Program
heading: Overview
text: A final program should make its measured values and mission routes easy for teammates to find. We can group imports and device setup, constants, functions, and launch calls in that order. This lesson reorganizes a practice program so a calibration change has one clear place to go.

title: Lesson F14.1: Organize the Program
heading: Worked example
text:
The threshold is named once and used by the mission function. The returned Boolean tells the caller what the sensor saw at the end of the straight drive; it does not by itself stop at a line.

~~~python
WHEEL_DIAMETER_MM = 56
AXLE_TRACK_MM = 112
LINE_THRESHOLD = 35

def line_mission():
    robot.straight(250)
    return color_sensor.reflection() < LINE_THRESHOLD

result = line_mission()
print("Line mission:", result)
~~~

title: Lesson F14.1: Organize the Program
heading: Simulator practice
text: Use the worked function or another practice route to arrange setup, constants, functions, and calls in four groups. Running before and after can check that organization changed without changing route behavior.

title: Lesson F14.1: Organize the Program
heading: On the robot
text: A teammate can read a printed program and locate the ports, wheel geometry, and main launch function. Any hard-to-find value is a candidate for a named constant.

title: Lesson F14.1: Organize the Program
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The revised file should show which values come from measurements and where they are used. A teammate's ability to find and explain one value is a useful check.

Reference: [Pybricks first robot program](https://pybricks.com/learn/making-programs/your-first-program/).

title: Lesson F14.2: Review Units and Stops
heading: Overview
text: Before the whole route runs, a code review can catch unit mistakes and missing stop conditions. DriveBase distance uses millimeters, angles use degrees, motor speeds use degrees per second, and waits use milliseconds. This lesson tests both a quick timeout and a normal approach to see whether the drive stops in each case.

title: Lesson F14.2: Review Units and Stops
heading: Worked example
text:
The loop ends when the object is close enough or the time limit is reached. A 2000 mm invalid reading is not treated separately in this sample, so a robust mission would check for it before interpreting the returned Boolean.

~~~python
def approach_safely(limit_ms):
    watch = StopWatch()
    robot.drive(100, 0)
    while distance_sensor.distance() > 150 and watch.time() < limit_ms:
        wait(10)
    robot.stop()
    return watch.time() < limit_ms

print("Cue found:", approach_safely(3000))
~~~

title: Lesson F14.2: Review Units and Stops
heading: Simulator practice
text: Put the worked `approach_safely()` function in the editor, then compare a 1 ms timeout with the normal 3000 ms limit. Both should reach `robot.stop()`, although their returned results may differ.

title: Lesson F14.2: Review Units and Stops
heading: On the robot
text: One teammate can read movement calls and units while another checks them against the field and port map. A missing sensor cue should also be tried at low speed.

title: Lesson F14.2: Review Units and Stops
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The review log should name each continuous drive's stop path and the failure cases tested. If a cue is absent, the timer, stop call, and returned result should agree.

Reference: [Pybricks UltrasonicSensor reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/ultrasonicsensor.html).

title: Lesson F14.3: Test the Whole Route
heading: Overview
text: After individual actions work, we can run them in match order. An integration test keeps the planned launch marks, attachment, and program selection together and records a result after each action. Those intermediate results can show where a full route first changes from the plan.

title: Lesson F14.3: Test the Whole Route
heading: Worked example
text:
The printed distance and tool angle are checkpoints after the approach and tool move. The final time describes the full sequence, but the field view is still needed to confirm home position and clearance.

~~~python
watch = StopWatch()
robot.straight(300)
print("Approach mm:", robot.distance())
attachment.run_angle(160, 60)
print("Tool deg:", attachment.angle())
robot.straight(-300)
print("Total ms:", watch.time())
~~~

title: Lesson F14.3: Test the Whole Route
heading: Simulator practice
text: Run the worked route three times from the same start. A table for approach, tool action, return, and elapsed time can reveal which result varies.

title: Lesson F14.3: Test the Whole Route
heading: On the robot
text: The match team should run the physical sequence with the intended attachment. Record the first incorrect action in each unsuccessful trial, including handling errors.

title: Lesson F14.3: Test the Whole Route
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The log should make the first incorrect result visible without relying only on final score. That action can then be retested from a known pose.

Reference: [Pybricks timing tools reference](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/tools/).

title: Lesson F14.4: Rehearse a Match
heading: Overview
text: A match rehearsal combines code with the people and handling around it. The team can practice program choice, launch alignment, attachments, and returns under the full 150 second clock. The current FIRST rulebook should guide real scoring and handling decisions.

title: Lesson F14.4: Rehearse a Match
heading: Worked example
text:
The loop prints two launch names and timestamps, then runs a simple action for each. It illustrates order and timing but does not model the physical reset or attachment handoff between launches.

~~~python
watch = StopWatch()
for mission_name in ["line", "target"]:
    print("Launch:", mission_name, "at ms:", watch.time())
    if mission_name == "line":
        robot.straight(250)
    else:
        attachment.run_angle(160, 60)
    robot.stop()
print("Rehearsal ms:", watch.time())
~~~

title: Lesson F14.4: Rehearse a Match
heading: Simulator practice
text: Use the worked loop as a timing outline, then add the planned route for each launch. The simulator clock can show the code time, while a full physical rehearsal also needs human handling time.

title: Lesson F14.4: Rehearse a Match
heading: On the robot
text: The actual match team should time a complete physical rehearsal with the intended attachments. Record handling delays and any recovery along with the drive time.

title: Lesson F14.4: Rehearse a Match
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The plan should be clear enough to follow at the field without reading the source. If the rehearsal exceeds the estimate, include its handling time in the budget and keep the last reliable program available.

Reference: [FIRST season materials](https://www.firstinspires.org/resources/library/fll/season-materials).

title: Lesson F14.5: Full Match Capstone
heading: Overview
text: The final project brings the route, robot measurements, sensor choices, and match plan together. The intended program should attempt the practice target and delivery objectives and return home. Repeated runs and a failed-cue test can show how well the plan works beyond one successful attempt.

title: Lesson F14.5: Full Match Capstone
heading: Worked example
text:
The sample function traces one generic-field route and prints its time. It provides a starting shape for the project; tested mission functions, sensor checks, and the team's own measurements still need to be added.

~~~python
def run_match():
    watch = StopWatch()
    print("Start light:", color_sensor.reflection())
    robot.straight(1380)
    attachment.run_angle(160, 90)
    robot.turn(180)
    robot.straight(430)
    robot.turn(90)
    robot.straight(180)
    robot.straight(480)
    robot.turn(90)
    robot.straight(830)
    attachment.run_angle(160, -90)
    robot.turn(180)
    robot.straight(1780)
    robot.turn(-90)
    robot.straight(660)
    robot.stop()
    print("Run ms:", watch.time())

run_match()
~~~

title: Lesson F14.5: Full Match Capstone
heading: Simulator practice
text: Replace the sample route with tested functions, then run under the 150 second clock. Record the target, delivery, and home results for every attempt.

title: Lesson F14.5: Full Match Capstone
heading: On the robot
text: Five complete physical trials can provide a success count, longest time, and a useful example of failure and recovery. Keep the last reliable source file with the robot's port map, geometry, thresholds, and launch marks.

title: Lesson F14.5: Full Match Capstone
heading: Check and adjust
text:
The final record should let a teammate reproduce the launch and explain the route's results. Include every trial, even when an objective fails, and use current FIRST materials for any real season score.

Reference: [FIRST season materials](https://www.firstinspires.org/resources/library/fll/season-materials).

title: FLL Pybricks Python Starter
heading: Overview
text:
Use this setup for course examples. Telemark's Python editor also provides the same names, but on a physical robot, connect only the devices you initialize, and change the port letters, motor direction, wheel diameter, and axle track to match your build.

~~~python
from pybricks.hubs import PrimeHub
from pybricks.pupdevices import Motor, ColorSensor, UltrasonicSensor
from pybricks.parameters import Port, Direction, Stop, Color
from pybricks.robotics import DriveBase
from pybricks.tools import wait, StopWatch

hub = PrimeHub()
left_motor = Motor(Port.A, Direction.COUNTERCLOCKWISE)
right_motor = Motor(Port.B)
robot = DriveBase(left_motor, right_motor, wheel_diameter=56, axle_track=112)
color_sensor = ColorSensor(Port.C)
distance_sensor = UltrasonicSensor(Port.D)
attachment = Motor(Port.E)
~~~

| Name | Course port | What it is| Unit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| left_motor | A | Left drive wheel | motor degrees |
| right_motor | B | Right drive wheel | motor degrees |
| color_sensor | C | Reflected light or color | percent or color value |
| distance_sensor | D | Range to object | millimeters |
| attachment | E | Mission tool | motor degrees |

The example wheel diameter is 56 mm and axle track is 112 mm, as specified in the [Pybricks example dimensions](https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/robotics.html). These are not measurements of your robot. You should measure both the wheel diameter and the axle track before physical route calibration. If your drive motors face the opposite direction, change the Direction setting after a small wheels-up test.

`robot.straight(300)` commands 300 mm of travel, and `robot.turn(90)` commands a 90 degree right turn. A call to `attachment.run_angle(180, 90)` rotates a tool by 90 degrees at 180 degrees per second, while `wait(100)` pauses for 100 milliseconds.

title: FLL Pybricks Python Starter
heading: Simulator limits
text: Telemark runs supported Pybricks-style Python locally in a worker, with a fixed starting pose and fixed objects on the practice field. The simulator does not upload code to a Hub or execute concurrent calls with `wait=False`, `run_task()`, Hub display and buttons, DataLog, or physical sensor lights. Lessons mark examples that require hardware.
